name: Garden of Eden
summary: Genesis presents Eden as the garden associated with the first human story. Its modern geographic location cannot be established, so this atlas deliberately does not place a normal map pin for Eden.

name: Mountains of Ararat
summary: The flood narrative says the ark came to rest on the “mountains of Ararat,” a regional expression rather than an identification of the modern summit called Mount Ararat.

name: Shinar
summary: A biblical regional name associated with southern Mesopotamia and the Babel narrative.

name: Babel / Babylon
summary: Genesis names Babel in Shinar in the tower narrative. The Hebrew name corresponds to Babylon, although the story’s literary and historical interpretation is distinct from the identification of the later city.

name: Ur
summary: The southern Mesopotamian city of Ur is the leading identification for the “Ur of the Chaldeans” named in the patriarchal narrative, though alternative proposals have existed.
aliases: Ur of the Chaldeans Tell el-Muqayyar

name: Haran
summary: Haran in upper Mesopotamia is a major stop in the Terah/Abraham narrative and later the setting of Jacob’s family story.

name: Damascus
summary: Damascus appears in Abraham’s pursuit narrative in Genesis 14 and serves as an important geographic reference point north of Canaan.

name: Canaan
summary: Canaan is the principal regional setting of the patriarchal narratives after Abraham’s migration from Haran.

name: Shechem
summary: Shechem is the first named Canaanite location in Abraham’s journey and later a major setting in Jacob’s story.

name: Bethel
summary: Bethel is prominent in both Abraham’s and Jacob’s narratives, including Jacob’s dream and later return.

name: Ai
summary: Ai is named near Bethel in Abraham’s route and later becomes important in Joshua. Its precise archaeological identification is debated.

name: Negev
summary: The Negev is the arid/semi-arid southern zone through which Abraham moves in Genesis.

name: Egypt
summary: Egypt appears repeatedly in Genesis: Abraham goes there during famine, Joseph rises to power there, and Jacob’s household eventually migrates there.

name: Hebron
summary: Hebron is one of the central patriarchal locations, associated with Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, and the family burial tradition.

name: Mamre
summary: Mamre is associated with Abraham’s encampment near Hebron and with several key Genesis scenes.

name: Salem
summary: Genesis 14 names Melchizedek as king of Salem. Salem has long been associated with Jerusalem, but Genesis itself does not explicitly state the equivalence.

name: Sodom
summary: Sodom is a major city in the Lot narratives, but its archaeological location remains disputed.

name: Gomorrah
summary: Gomorrah is paired with Sodom in Genesis, but no modern archaeological identification is secure enough to map as a point.

name: Zoar
summary: Zoar is the small city to which Lot flees in Genesis 19. Its broad setting near the Dead Sea is plausible, but exact identification is uncertain.

name: Plain of the Jordan
summary: The well-watered Jordan plain is central to Lot’s choice in Genesis 13. The narrative geography points toward the Jordan/Dead Sea basin, but exact ancient extents and settlement relations are debated.

name: Beersheba
summary: Beersheba is a recurring patriarchal center associated with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

name: Gerar
summary: Gerar is associated with Abimelech in the Abraham and Isaac narratives. Its exact location is not completely settled.

name: Beer-lahai-roi
summary: A well associated with Hagar and later Isaac. Genesis locates it between Kadesh and Bered, but the site has not been securely identified.

name: Moriah
summary: Genesis 22 sends Abraham to the “land of Moriah.” 2 Chronicles 3:1 later names Mount Moriah as the site of Solomon’s temple in Jerusalem, creating the canonical basis for the traditional Jerusalem identification.

name: Paddan-aram
summary: The regional setting of Jacob’s years with Laban, closely associated with Haran in the Genesis narrative.

name: Gilead
summary: The highland region east of the Jordan forms the setting for Jacob’s encounter with Laban on his return from Paddan-aram.

name: Mahanaim
summary: Jacob names Mahanaim after an encounter with the “camp of God.” The ancient site’s exact modern identification is uncertain.

name: Jabbok River
summary: The Jabbok is the river/wadi associated with Jacob’s night encounter before meeting Esau.

name: Peniel / Penuel
summary: Jacob names the place Peniel after wrestling through the night near the Jabbok. Exact site identification remains uncertain.

name: Succoth
summary: Jacob settles temporarily at Succoth after meeting Esau. The site lies east of the Jordan, but exact identification is debated.

name: Dothan
summary: Dothan is where Joseph finds his brothers before being sold and taken toward Egypt.

name: Goshen
summary: Goshen is the region of Egypt in which Joseph settles Jacob’s household according to Genesis.

name: On / Heliopolis
summary: Joseph marries Asenath, daughter of Potiphera priest of On. On is securely identified with ancient Heliopolis in the Cairo area.

name: Seir / Edom
summary: Seir/Edom is associated with Esau and his descendants in Genesis.

name: Rameses / Pi-Ramesses
summary: Exodus names Rameses as a departure point and one of the store-city names associated with Israelite labor. The major Ramesside royal city Pi-Ramesses is securely located at Qantir, but the biblical toponym does not by itself fix the date or route of the Exodus.

name: Pithom
summary: Exodus names Pithom alongside Rameses. Its identification is disputed, with Tell el-Maskhuta and Tell er-Retaba among the principal proposals in Wadi Tumilat.

name: Tell el-Maskhuta
summary: An archaeological site in Wadi Tumilat often proposed as Pithom. It is shown as a candidate site, not as the settled biblical identification.

name: Tell er-Retaba
summary: A fortified settlement in Wadi Tumilat and another major candidate for biblical Pithom.

name: Wadi Tumilat
summary: An east–west corridor across the eastern Nile Delta that is important for reconstructing travel between the Delta and the Sinai approaches.

name: Succoth (Exodus)
summary: The first station named after departure from Rameses. It is generally placed somewhere in or near the eastern Delta/Wadi Tumilat system, but no site is securely established.

name: Etham
summary: A wilderness-edge station named after Succoth. Its location is unknown.

name: Pi-hahiroth
summary: An Exodus station associated with the sea-crossing narrative. Its location is unknown and depends heavily on broader route theories.

name: Migdol (Exodus)
summary: A place-name meaning “tower” or associated with a fortified point in the sea-crossing narrative. Several Egyptian frontier locations have been proposed, but no unique identification is secure.

name: Baal-zephon
summary: A place named opposite the Israelite camp before the sea crossing. Its precise location is unknown.

name: Yam Suph / Sea Crossing Region
summary: The Hebrew expression yam sûp̄ is traditionally rendered “Red Sea” and often discussed as “Sea of Reeds.” The specific body of water crossed in Exodus cannot be fixed with confidence.

name: Marah
summary: A wilderness station where the water is described as bitter. Its location is not securely known.

name: Elim
summary: A wilderness station associated with twelve springs and seventy palm trees. Its precise modern location is unknown.

name: Wilderness of Sin
summary: A wilderness region named between Elim and Sinai. It should not be confused with the later “Wilderness of Zin.”

name: Rephidim
summary: A station before Sinai associated with water from the rock and conflict with Amalek. Its location is not securely known.

name: Mount Sinai / Horeb
summary: The mountain of the covenant in Exodus. Its location is unknown; traditions and scholarly proposals range across the Sinai Peninsula and beyond.

name: Jebel Musa
summary: The traditional Mount Sinai in southern Sinai, beside St Catherine’s Monastery. It is mapped as a traditional identification only.

name: Har Karkom
summary: A mountain in the southern Negev proposed by some scholars as Mount Sinai/Horeb. The proposal is controversial and not widely accepted as established.

name: Hazeroth
summary: A wilderness station associated with Miriam and Aaron’s challenge to Moses. Its exact location is unknown.

name: Kibroth-hattaavah
summary: A wilderness station named in Numbers in connection with the quail episode. Its modern location is unknown.

name: Kadesh-barnea
summary: A major wilderness location associated with the spies, extended encampment, and the southern approach to Canaan. ʿAin el-Qudeirat is the leading modern identification, though the relationship between the archaeological remains and the narrative periods is complex.

name: Hormah
summary: A southern-Canaan/Negev place associated with conflict in Numbers and later in Judges. Its precise site identification remains debated.

name: Arad
summary: An ancient city site in the northern Negev. Tel Arad is securely identified with later biblical Arad, though the relationship between the archaeological sequence and the conquest narrative requires caution.

name: Mount Hor
summary: The mountain where Numbers places Aaron’s death. Jabal Harun near Petra is the dominant later tradition, but the biblical mountain is not securely identified.

name: Ezion-geber
summary: A Red Sea port/place near Elath mentioned in the wilderness itinerary and later monarchic narratives. Tell el-Kheleifeh was long identified with Ezion-geber, but precise identification and function have been debated.

name: Midian
summary: A biblical regional/people-name associated with Moses’ flight, Jethro, and later conflicts. Its geographic extent varied and cannot be drawn as a precise modern border.

name: Moab
summary: A Transjordanian region east of the Dead Sea associated with Balak, Balaam, and Israel’s final approach to the Jordan.

name: Arnon / Wadi Mujib
summary: The Arnon is securely identified with Wadi Mujib, a major canyon entering the Dead Sea from the east.

name: Dibon
summary: An important Moabite city securely identified with Dhiban, later famous for the Mesha Stele.

name: Heshbon
summary: A Transjordanian city associated in Numbers and Deuteronomy with Sihon. Tell Hesban is the traditional archaeological identification, though the site’s Late Bronze/Iron Age sequence complicates direct narrative correlation.

name: Plains of Moab
summary: The biblical staging area east of the Jordan opposite Jericho where Numbers and Deuteronomy place Israel before entry into Canaan.

name: Mount Nebo
summary: The ridge east of the Jordan traditionally and geographically associated with Moses’ final view of the land.

name: Jordan Crossing Opposite Jericho
summary: Joshua describes Israel crossing the Jordan opposite Jericho. The river corridor is known, but the exact crossing point is not securely identified.

name: Jericho / Tell es-Sultan
summary: The ancient settlement mound of Jericho is securely located at Tell es-Sultan. The archaeological chronology of its Late Bronze occupation/destruction and its relationship to Joshua 6 remain major subjects of debate.

name: Gilgal (Joshua)
summary: The first encampment west of the Jordan in Joshua and a recurring place-name in the narratives. Several sites near Jericho have been proposed; no identification is secure.

name: Gibeon / el-Jib
summary: Ancient Gibeon is securely identified with el-Jib northwest of Jerusalem, supported by archaeology and inscribed jar handles.

name: Valley of Aijalon
summary: A valley west of the central highlands, named in Joshua’s battle poem. The valley is geographically identifiable, though the event’s precise battlefield movements are not reconstructable.

name: Hazor / Tel Hazor
summary: The largest major Canaanite center in the southern Levant, securely identified with Tel Hazor. Joshua 11 associates it with a northern coalition and destruction; archaeological destruction levels exist, but their narrative correlation is debated.

name: Waters of Merom
summary: A geographic name in Joshua 11 associated with the northern battle. The exact body of water or locality is uncertain; identification with the Hula region is common but not definitive.

name: Shiloh / Khirbet Seilun
summary: A central hill-country sanctuary and assembly place in Joshua and Judges. Khirbet Seilun is the accepted location of ancient Shiloh.

name: Mount Ebal
summary: The mountain north of Shechem associated in Deuteronomy and Joshua with covenant ceremony. The mountain itself is securely identified; interpretation of a prominent Iron Age structure on it is debated.

name: Mount Gerizim
summary: The mountain south of Shechem paired with Ebal in the covenant blessings and curses.

name: Timnath-serah
summary: Joshua’s inheritance and burial place in the hill country of Ephraim. Khirbet Tibnah is a common proposal, but the identification is not absolute.

name: Megiddo / Tel Megiddo
summary: A major fortified city controlling routes through the Jezreel Valley. Judges 5 names Megiddo in the poetic battle setting.

name: Taanach / Tell Taʿannek
summary: A Canaanite city near Megiddo, named in Judges 5 and the territorial traditions.

name: Beth-shean / Tell el-Husn
summary: A major city in the Jordan Valley with strong Egyptian presence in the Late Bronze Age; Judges names it among cities not taken by Manasseh.

name: Kedesh in Naphtali
summary: The northern city associated with Barak. Tel Kedesh is the leading identification.

name: Mount Tabor
summary: A prominent Lower Galilee mountain where Deborah instructs Barak to assemble forces.

name: Kishon River
summary: The river draining the Jezreel Valley toward the Mediterranean and associated with the battle in Judges 4–5.

name: Harosheth-hagoyim
summary: Sisera’s base in Judges 4. Its exact location is disputed, and proposed sites depend on interpretation of the Kishon battle geography.

name: Ophrah of the Abiezrites
summary: Gideon’s home in Judges 6. Its exact location is unknown.

name: Spring of Harod
summary: The spring where Gideon selects his fighting force before confronting Midian. ʿAin Jalud is the common identification.

name: Jezreel Valley
summary: A major east–west lowland corridor and repeated arena of conflict in Judges.

name: Mizpah of Gilead
summary: A meeting place associated with Jephthah in Judges 10–11. Its exact site is disputed among Transjordanian proposals.

name: Zorah
summary: A town in the Shephelah associated with Samson’s family. Tel Zorʿa is the accepted/probable identification.

name: Eshtaol
summary: A town paired with Zorah in the Samson narratives. Its identification is probable in the same Shephelah district, but less secure than major tells.

name: Timnah (Samson)
summary: A Philistine-border town in the Samson narratives, commonly identified with Tel Batash in the Sorek Valley.

name: Valley of Sorek
summary: The valley associated with Delilah in Judges 16, forming a natural corridor between the Philistine plain and Judahite highlands.

name: Gaza
summary: One of the principal Philistine cities and the setting of Samson’s final episode. Ancient Gaza lies beneath and around the modern city, so the historical city is secure even though exact Iron Age urban boundaries are not.

name: Ashkelon
summary: A major Philistine coastal city named in Samson’s story. Its archaeological site is securely identified.

name: Ashdod
summary: One of the Philistine pentapolis cities, important to the Judges-era political landscape even where individual narratives focus elsewhere.

name: Ekron / Tel Miqne
summary: A Philistine pentapolis city securely identified with Tel Miqne, with strong inscriptional support from a later Iron Age royal dedicatory inscription.

name: Gath / Tell es-Safi
summary: One of the major Philistine cities, securely/probably identified with Tell es-Safi.

name: Lehi / Ramath-lehi
summary: A place in Judah associated with Samson’s battle and the spring called En-hakkore. Its modern location is unknown.

name: Edom
summary: A Transjordanian/southern highland region associated with the descendants of Esau. Its geographic core south and southeast of the Dead Sea is clear, while political borders and the chronology of Edomite state formation changed over time.

name: Ammon
summary: A Transjordanian region centered east of the Jordan around the Amman/Rabbah highlands, especially important in Deuteronomy and the Jephthah narrative.

name: Bashan
summary: A broad region east and northeast of the Sea of Galilee, associated in Numbers and Deuteronomy with Og and later Transjordanian territorial traditions.

name: Debir / Kiriath-sepher
summary: A hill-country town captured in the Othniel tradition. Several archaeological sites have been proposed; no identification is sufficiently secure here for a normal pin.

name: Thebez
summary: A town where Abimelech is mortally wounded in Judges 9. Modern Tubas is a common geographic proposal, but the equation is not fully secure.

name: Dan / Laish
summary: The northern city called Laish before the Danite migration and later Dan. Tel Dan is the securely identified archaeological site of ancient Dan/Laish.

name: Bethlehem of Judah
summary: A Judean hill-country town that appears at the opening of Judges 17 and in the Levite narrative of Judges 19. The town’s location is secure, though individual episode locations within it are not recoverable.

name: Gibeah of Benjamin
summary: The Benjaminite town central to Judges 19–20. Tell el-Ful is the traditional and leading candidate for Gibeah, but the exact identification and occupation history require caution.
aliases: Gibeah Gibeah of Saul Tell el-Ful (proposal)

name: Mizpah of Benjamin
summary: An assembly point in Judges 20–21. Tell en-Nasbeh is the leading archaeological identification for Mizpah of Benjamin, though the map keeps it at probable rather than absolute confidence.

name: Jabesh-gilead
summary: A Transjordanian town involved in the aftermath of the Benjaminite civil war. Proposed archaeological identifications exist, but no single site is secure enough for a normal pin in this release.

name: Hill Country of Ephraim
summary: A central highland region that forms the setting for multiple Judges traditions, including Ehud’s rallying point and the Levite of Judges 19.

name: Ramathaim-zophim
summary: Samuel's family home in 1 Samuel 1. The precise modern identification is unresolved, so the atlas preserves the textual place without a pin.

name: Ramah of Samuel
summary: Samuel's base after the Shiloh period and a recurring location in the Saul narratives. The identification with er-Ram north of Jerusalem is common but not certain.

name: Aphek / Tel Afek
summary: The Philistine camp location before the battle in which the ark was captured. Ancient Aphek is securely identified with Tel Afek near the Yarkon headwaters.

name: Ebenezer (1 Samuel)
summary: The Israelite camp and battle location in 1 Samuel 4. The text places it opposite Philistine Aphek, but no modern site can be identified confidently.

name: Beth-shemesh / Tel Beth Shemesh
summary: The border-town to which the ark returns from Philistine territory in 1 Samuel 6. The ancient city is securely located at Tel Beth Shemesh.
aliases: Beth-shemesh Tell er-Rumeileh Tel Beth Shemesh

name: Kiriath-jearim
summary: A hill-country town where the ark remains before David brings it toward Jerusalem. The Deir el-Azar / Tel Qiryat Ye'arim hill is the leading archaeological identification.
aliases: Kiriath Jearim Kiriath-baal Deir el-Azar / Tel Qiryat Ye’arim

name: Gilgal in Samuel
summary: A recurring assembly and cultic place in the Samuel narratives. Whether every Samuel reference points to the same Gilgal as Joshua's encampment is uncertain.

name: Valley of Elah
summary: The broad valley between the Judean highlands and Philistine plain that forms the setting of the David and Goliath narrative.

name: Socoh of Judah
summary: A Judean town named beside Azekah in the Philistine deployment before David's encounter with Goliath.

name: Azekah / Tel Azekah
summary: A fortified hill on the western approaches to Judah, named in the Elah Valley deployment.

name: Nob
summary: The priestly town visited by David in 1 Samuel 21. Its general setting near Jerusalem is likely, but the exact archaeological site remains unresolved.

name: Adullam
summary: A Judean lowland stronghold associated with David's fugitive period. The town is commonly placed near Khirbet esh-Sheikh Madhkur, while the cave itself cannot be identified.
aliases: Cave of Adullam Khirbet esh-Sheikh Madhkur (proposal)

name: Keilah
summary: A fortified town rescued by David from Philistine attack and later left when Saul approached.

name: Ziph of Judah
summary: A settlement and wilderness district south of Hebron central to Saul's pursuit of David.

name: Maon of Judah
summary: A town south of Hebron associated with the wilderness where David evades Saul and with Nabal's household.

name: Carmel of Judah
summary: A Judean hill-country town near Maon associated with Nabal and Abigail; it is distinct from Mount Carmel in northern Israel.

name: En-gedi
summary: An oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea associated with David's refuge from Saul.

name: Wilderness of Ziph
summary: The rugged hill-country/desert-margin district around Ziph where David hides from Saul. The marker is a regional orientation only.

name: Wilderness of Maon
summary: A southern Judean wilderness district in the pursuit narratives, represented as a broad orientation rather than a boundary.

name: Ziklag
summary: A town granted to David by Achish of Gath. Numerous sites in the northern Negev and Shephelah have been proposed, but no identification has achieved consensus.

name: Besor Brook / Wadi Gaza
summary: The watercourse crossed during David's pursuit of Amalekite raiders. The modern Besor/Wadi Gaza system provides the regional anchor; the exact crossing is unknown.

name: Mount Gilboa
summary: The ridge south-east of the Jezreel Valley where Saul and his sons die in battle against the Philistines.

name: Shunem
summary: A settlement on the northern edge of the Jezreel Valley where the Philistines camp before Saul's final battle.

name: Endor
summary: The place where Saul consults a medium before the battle on Gilboa. The ancient settlement is usually sought near the modern name-survival area north of the Jezreel Valley.

name: Jerusalem
summary: The highland city captured by David and made the political center of his kingdom; it becomes the central city of the Solomon narratives.

name: Southeastern Ridge / “City of David” Archaeological Zone
summary: The narrow ridge south of the Temple Mount that preserves the earliest urban core of Jerusalem. Modern archaeology commonly calls it the City of David, while the biblical phrase can function differently in different texts.
aliases: City of David archaeological zone Southeastern Hill Southeastern Ridge

name: Zion — Biblical Toponym
summary: In 2 Samuel 5, Zion names the stronghold David captures and associates with the City of David. Later biblical usage expands toward Jerusalem and the temple, so the atlas treats Zion as a changing toponym rather than one eternal GPS point.
aliases: Zion Fortress of Zion Mount Zion

name: Kidron Valley
summary: The valley immediately east of ancient Jerusalem, crossed by David as he flees Absalom.

name: Mount of Olives
summary: The ridge east of Jerusalem ascended by David during Absalom's revolt and prominent in later biblical history.

name: Valley of Rephaim
summary: A valley southwest of Jerusalem associated with Philistine deployments after David's accession.

name: Baal-perazim
summary: A battle locality named after David's victory over the Philistines near the Rephaim Valley. Its exact location cannot be recovered.

name: Gihon Spring
summary: Jerusalem's principal ancient spring, used as the setting for Solomon's public anointing in 1 Kings 1.

name: Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif
summary: The elevated sacred precinct north of the southeastern ridge, traditionally and historically associated with the First and Second Temples. Direct archaeological excavation of the temple footprint is not available.

name: First Temple — Biblical Building Site
summary: The temple Solomon is said to build in Jerusalem. The atlas keeps it searchable and links it to the Temple Mount tradition but does not draw an exact footprint as an archaeological fact.

name: Threshing Floor of Araunah / Ornan
summary: The location where David erects an altar after the census plague and which Chronicles later connects with the temple site. No independent archaeological point can be assigned.
aliases: Araunah’s threshing floor Ornan’s threshing floor

name: Rabbah of the Ammonites / Amman
summary: The Ammonite capital besieged by Joab and David in 2 Samuel. Its location at modern Amman is secure, though the exact Iron Age urban extent is not.

name: Geshur
summary: A small polity in the southern Golan / Bashan region associated with Absalom's maternal family and exile. Its political boundaries are not precisely recoverable.

name: Bahurim
summary: A settlement east or northeast of Jerusalem encountered in the Absalom narratives. Its exact site remains uncertain.

name: Forest of Ephraim
summary: The battlefield where Absalom's forces are defeated. Despite the name, the narrative context is east of the Jordan around Mahanaim; the exact location is unknown.

name: Gezer / Tel Gezer
summary: A major city at the Aijalon approaches. 1 Kings associates its transfer and building activity with Solomon; archaeology confirms major Iron Age occupation while the dating and attribution of specific gates/structures remain debated.

name: Tyre
summary: The Phoenician port city associated with Hiram's diplomatic, timber, and craft relationship with David and Solomon.

name: Sidon
summary: A principal Phoenician coastal city and regional reference point in the monarchy narratives.

name: Ophir
summary: A source of gold associated with Solomon's maritime trade. Proposals range across Arabia, the Red Sea, East Africa, and beyond; no consensus location exists.

name: Sheba / Saba — Southern Arabian Context
summary: The Queen of Sheba narrative points toward the Sabaean cultural world of southern Arabia. The marker uses the Marib region as a broad cultural anchor, not as a claim about the queen's palace or itinerary.

name: Michmash / Mukhmas area
summary: A Benjaminite town east of the central ridge and the principal Philistine/Israelite theater in 1 Samuel 13–14. The modern name Mukhmas preserves the ancient toponym, though the precise Iron Age settlement footprint is not mapped here as certain.

name: Geba of Benjamin
summary: A Benjaminite town opposite the Michmash area in the Saul/Jonathan narratives. The modern village Jabaʿ is commonly associated with ancient Geba.

name: Pass of Michmash / Wadi Suweinit context
summary: The steep ravine landscape between the Geba and Michmash areas associated with Jonathan’s attack. The broad topography is identifiable, while the named crags Bozez and Seneh are not securely fixed to individual rocks.

name: Kingdom of Israel (Northern Kingdom)
summary: The northern polity that emerges after the division of the monarchy. Samaria becomes its capital under Omri; biblical and extra-biblical sources also use “Israel,” “Samaria,” and Assyrian dynastic labels in different contexts.

name: Kingdom of Judah
summary: The southern kingdom centered on Jerusalem after the division of the monarchy. Its territorial reach varied significantly through the Iron Age.

name: Aram-Damascus
summary: The Aramean kingdom centered on Damascus, a major rival and occasional ally of Israel before Assyrian annexation in the eighth century BCE.

name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
summary: The imperial power that progressively intervened in Syria-Palestine, annexed Damascus and northern Israelite territories, ended the Northern Kingdom, and campaigned against Judah.

name: Samaria / Sebaste
summary: Capital founded by Omri on a purchased hill and the political center of the Northern Kingdom until its Assyrian capture.

name: Tirzah / Tell el-Far‘ah (North)
summary: Early capital of the Northern Kingdom before Omri founded Samaria. Tell el-Far‘ah (North) is the leading identification.

name: Jezreel / Tel Jezreel
summary: Royal center in the Jezreel Valley associated with Ahab, Jezebel, Naboth, and Jehu’s coup.

name: Mount Carmel
summary: The coastal mountain ridge that provides the setting for Elijah’s confrontation with the prophets of Baal in 1 Kings 18.

name: Brook Kerith / Cherith
summary: The brook or wadi east of the Jordan where Elijah is told to hide during the drought narrative.

name: Zarephath / Sarepta
summary: Phoenician coastal town between Tyre and Sidon where Elijah stays with a widow during the drought.

name: Tishbe in Gilead
summary: Elijah is introduced as a Tishbite from Gilead. The exact settlement is not securely identified.

name: Abel-meholah
summary: Home region of Elisha when Elijah calls him. Its exact location in the Jordan Valley is debated.

name: Ramoth-gilead
summary: Strategic Transjordanian city repeatedly contested by Israel and Aram and the starting setting for Jehu’s coup.

name: Aphek of the Aramean wars
summary: Aphek named in Ahab’s conflict with Ben-hadad. This is not automatically the same Aphek as the Philistine-camp site near the Yarkon.

name: Jordan River
summary: The major river running from the Hula/Sea of Galilee system to the Dead Sea, repeatedly central to Elisha’s narratives.

name: Kir-hareseth / Kir of Moab
summary: Moabite stronghold attacked in the coalition campaign of 2 Kings 3, commonly associated with the Kerak area.

name: Qarqar / Tell Qarqur
summary: North Syrian battle location where Shalmaneser III fought a western coalition in 853 BCE. Tell Qarqur is the leading identification.

name: Tekoa / Khirbet Tuqu‘
summary: Judean hill-country town associated with the prophet Amos.

name: Moresheth-gath
summary: Shephelah town associated with the prophet Micah. Proposed identifications exist, but the exact site remains uncertain.

name: Joppa / Jaffa
summary: Ancient Mediterranean port from which Jonah boards a ship bound for Tarshish in the narrative.

name: Tarshish
summary: Distant maritime destination named in Jonah 1. Its identification is disputed and should not be reduced to a single point such as Tartessos without qualification.

name: Mediterranean Sea
summary: The Mediterranean maritime world connecting Phoenicia, Philistia, Joppa, Egypt, Anatolia, Cyprus, and the wider ancient world.

name: Nineveh
summary: Major Assyrian city on the Tigris opposite modern Mosul; later imperial capital and the destination of Jonah’s commission.

name: Kalhu / Calah / Nimrud
summary: Major Neo-Assyrian royal city south of Nineveh, associated with imperial administration and monuments such as the Black Obelisk.

name: Dur-Sharrukin / Khorsabad
summary: Royal city founded by Sargon II near Nineveh, relevant to the imperial context following the fall of Samaria.

name: Gozan / Guzana / Tell Halaf
summary: Upper Mesopotamian city and region named among destinations of deported Israelites after the fall of Samaria.

name: Habor / Khabur River
summary: Euphrates tributary region named in the Assyrian deportation notices.

name: Halah
summary: One of the locations named in the Assyrian deportation formula for the Northern Kingdom. Its precise identification remains uncertain.

name: Media
summary: Broad Iranian highland region whose cities are named among Assyrian deportation destinations in Kings.
aliases: land of the Medes cities of the Medes

name: Lachish / Tel Lachish
summary: Major fortified city of Judah captured by Sennacherib in 701 BCE and vividly represented in Assyrian palace reliefs.

name: Libnah (Judah)
summary: Judean town mentioned when the Assyrian field commander leaves Lachish in the 701 BCE campaign narrative. Its precise archaeological identification remains debated.

name: Siloam Tunnel / Hezekiah’s Tunnel
summary: Rock-cut water tunnel carrying Gihon Spring water toward the southern part of ancient Jerusalem, commonly associated with Hezekiah’s preparations.

name: Conduit of the Upper Pool / Fuller’s Field road
summary: Jerusalem topographic reference in Isaiah’s encounter with Ahaz and later in the Assyrian envoy narrative.

name: Anathoth
summary: Priestly town associated with Jeremiah’s family and land purchase; commonly identified with the village area of Anata northeast of Jerusalem.

name: Valley of Hinnom
summary: Valley adjoining Jerusalem, central to Jeremiah’s denunciation of Topheth and later Gehenna traditions.
aliases: Ge Hinnom Valley of Ben Hinnom

name: Topheth
summary: Cultic place condemned by Jeremiah in the Valley of Ben Hinnom.

name: Ketef Hinnom
summary: Jerusalem burial-cave complex where two small silver amulets preserving wording related to the priestly blessing were discovered.

name: Ramat Rahel
summary: Major administrative and elite complex south of Jerusalem with important late Iron Age, Babylonian, and Persian-period phases.

name: Riblah
summary: Northern Syrian headquarters where the biblical narrative places Nebuchadnezzar during the final judgment on Zedekiah and Judean officials.
aliases: Riblah in the land of Hamath

name: Carchemish
summary: Major Euphrates city where Babylonian and Egyptian forces fought in 605 BCE, a crucial chronological anchor for the end of Judah’s independence.

name: Hamath
summary: Major Syrian city/region on the Orontes corridor, useful for understanding Riblah and northward imperial routes.

name: Tahpanhes
summary: Eastern Nile Delta site associated with the Judean refugees and Jeremiah after Gedaliah’s assassination.

name: Memphis (Noph)
summary: Ancient Egyptian capital region named Noph in Jeremiah; important context for Judean communities in Egypt.

name: Pathros / Upper Egypt
summary: Regional name for Upper Egypt, included among places where Judeans are addressed in Jeremiah 44.

name: Migdol in Jeremiah’s Egyptian setting
summary: An Egyptian place named with Tahpanhes, Noph, and Pathros in Jeremiah 44; multiple eastern-Delta sites named “Migdol/tower” complicate exact identification.

name: Perath in Jeremiah 13
summary: Place/river term in Jeremiah’s linen-belt sign action. The Hebrew commonly denotes the Euphrates, but the extraordinary travel implied has generated alternative local proposals.

name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
summary: Mesopotamian empire under Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II that defeated Egypt’s position in Syria-Palestine and conquered Judah.

name: Nebuchadnezzar II’s Southern Palace at Babylon
summary: Excavated Neo-Babylonian royal palace complex at Babylon, useful context for the court world imagined in Daniel.

name: Nippur
summary: Major Babylonian city and administrative landscape south-east of Babylon; important for locating exilic settlement evidence in central/southern Babylonia.

name: Kebar Canal
summary: Babylonian waterway beside which Ezekiel locates himself among the exiles.

name: Tel-abib in Babylonia
summary: Settlement by the Kebar where Ezekiel says he sat among the exiles. It is unrelated to the modern Israeli city Tel Aviv.

name: Al-Yahudu (“Town of Judah”)
summary: Settlement known from cuneiform documents involving Judeans in Babylonia, important independent evidence for exile-community life.

name: Judean Exile Settlement Zone in Babylonia
summary: Generalized central/southern Babylonian landscape where Judean exiles are attested by biblical and cuneiform sources.

name: Euphrates River
summary: Major Mesopotamian river structuring imperial travel and settlement; named explicitly in Jeremiah and elsewhere.

name: Tigris River
summary: Major Mesopotamian river used as the setting of Daniel 10.

name: Plain of Dura
summary: Plain in the province of Babylon where Daniel 3 sets Nebuchadnezzar’s image. Numerous “Duru/Dura” place-names prevent a secure identification.

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
summary: Empire founded by Cyrus II that conquered Babylon in 539 BCE and governed Judah/Yehud through the Persian period.

name: Susa
summary: Major Elamite and Achaemenid royal center; primary setting of Esther and a visionary setting in Daniel 8.

name: Ulai Canal
summary: Watercourse in Daniel 8’s Susa vision.

name: Ecbatana
summary: Median/Persian royal city called Achmetha in Ezra 6, where the narrative says Cyrus’s memorandum was found.

name: Persepolis
summary: Monumental Achaemenid royal center founded under Darius I; not named in the Hebrew Bible but essential context for the Persian imperial world.

name: Pasargadae
summary: Early Achaemenid royal center associated with Cyrus II, useful for understanding the Persian world behind Ezra.

name: Elam / Susiana
summary: Southwestern Iranian region containing Susa, named in Daniel 8’s literary setting.

name: Yehud (Persian-period Judah)
summary: Small Persian-period province centered on Jerusalem, the political setting of much of Ezra and Nehemiah.

name: Beyond the River (Abar-Nahara)
summary: Western Persian administrative designation used in Ezra for the territory west of the Euphrates.

name: Ahava
summary: Gathering place where Ezra assembles the returning group before departure toward Jerusalem.

name: Casiphia
summary: Place from which Ezra requests Levites and temple servants during the Ahava encampment.

name: Elephantine
summary: Island on the Nile with a fifth-century BCE Judean/Jewish military community and temple documented in Aramaic papyri.

name: Early Second Temple footprint
summary: Temple completed in the reign of Darius I according to Ezra. Its broad location belongs on the Temple Mount, but the exact Persian-period architectural footprint is not independently recoverable.

name: Nehemiah’s wall circuit
summary: Wall and gate system rebuilt in Nehemiah’s narrative. Archaeology illuminates Persian-period Jerusalem, but the exact line and identification of every named gate remain debated.

name: Cush / Nubia
summary: Nile-valley region south of Egypt referenced in prophetic and Persian-imperial biblical geography.

name: Thebes (No-Amon)
summary: Major Egyptian city invoked in Nahum as an example of a seemingly powerful city that had nevertheless fallen.

name: Teman in Edom
summary: Edomite place/region used in prophetic literature as a poetic-geographic representative of Edom.

name: Pella
summary: Macedonian royal center associated with Philip II and Alexander III. The archaeological site lies near modern Pella in northern Greece.

name: Granicus River battle region
summary: Region of Alexander’s first major battle against Persian forces in Asia Minor in 334 BCE.

name: Issus battle region
summary: Regional anchor for the 333 BCE battle between Alexander and Darius III near the Gulf of Issus.

name: Alexandria
summary: City founded by Alexander on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast and developed into the major Ptolemaic capital and Jewish diaspora center.

name: Antioch on the Orontes
summary: Seleucid royal foundation that became one of the great cities of the Hellenistic and Roman eastern Mediterranean.

name: Seleucia Pieria
summary: Port city serving Antioch and the Seleucid state on the northeastern Mediterranean.

name: Ptolemais / Akko
summary: Ancient coastal city renamed Ptolemais in the Hellenistic period and repeatedly important in Seleucid and Hasmonean politics.

name: Panium / Paneas
summary: Sanctuary and settlement area at the foot of Mount Hermon, near the 200 BCE battle that shifted Coele-Syria from Ptolemaic to Seleucid control.

name: Modein
summary: Town associated in 1 Maccabees with Mattathias and the beginning of the revolt against Seleucid policies.

name: Emmaus (Nicopolis)
summary: Hellenistic-period Emmaus in the Aijalon approaches, associated with Judas Maccabeus’s victory over a Seleucid force in 165 BCE.

name: Beth-horon
summary: Strategic ascent on the route from the coastal plain toward Jerusalem, important in Maccabean warfare.

name: Beth-zur
summary: Fortified Judean site south of Jerusalem, repeatedly contested during the Maccabean revolt.

name: Beth-zechariah
summary: Battle locality south of Jerusalem associated with the Seleucid campaign against Judas Maccabeus in 162 BCE.

name: Adasa
summary: Locality north of Jerusalem associated with Judas Maccabeus’s defeat of Nicanor in 161 BCE.

name: Elasa
summary: Battle locality where Judas Maccabeus was killed fighting Bacchides in 160 BCE.

name: Jerusalem Acra
summary: Seleucid fortress/garrison complex in Jerusalem central to the Maccabean narratives.

name: Mount Gerizim sanctuary precinct
summary: Archaeological sanctuary and settlement complex on Mount Gerizim associated with the Samaritan community in Persian and Hellenistic periods.

name: Idumea
summary: Hellenistic successor region to biblical Edom in southern Judea/Shephelah, with important centers such as Maresha.

name: Maresha / Marisa
summary: Major Hellenistic city in Idumea with a diverse population and extensive archaeological remains.

name: Adora
summary: Idumean settlement/fortified center associated with Hasmonean expansion south of Judea.

name: Jamnia / Yavneh
summary: Coastal-plain city contested by Hasmonean and neighboring powers and later important in Roman-period Jewish history.

name: Dor
summary: Ancient Mediterranean port city north of Caesarea, part of the Hellenistic and Hasmonean coastal political landscape.

name: Caesarea Maritima
summary: Herod’s monumental harbor city on the Mediterranean, developed from Strato’s Tower and dedicated in the late first century BCE.

name: Herodium
summary: Herod’s palace-fortress and later mausoleum complex southeast of Jerusalem.

name: Masada
summary: Desert fortress overlooking the Dead Sea, enlarged dramatically under Herod after earlier Hasmonean use.

name: Jericho Herodian palace complex
summary: Winter-palace landscape west of ancient Jericho used and expanded by Hasmonean and Herodian rulers.

name: Khirbet Qumran
summary: Second Temple period settlement near the northwest Dead Sea, adjacent to caves where many Dead Sea Scrolls were found.

name: Leontopolis Jewish temple region
summary: Egyptian locality associated by Josephus with a Jewish temple founded by Onias in the Ptolemaic period.

name: Petra
summary: Nabataean capital and monumental caravan center in southern Transjordan.

name: Avdat / Oboda
summary: Nabataean caravan station and later town on the incense route through the Negev.

name: Rome
summary: Capital of the Roman Republic and, under Augustus, the imperial center that increasingly shaped Judean politics.

name: Actium battle region
summary: Naval battle region in western Greece where Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BCE.

name: Rhodes
summary: Major eastern Mediterranean island/city where Herod met Octavian after Actium according to Josephus.

name: Samaria / Sebaste
summary: Herodian refoundation of the older city of Samaria, renamed Sebaste in honor of Augustus.

name: Hasmonean palace in Jerusalem
summary: Royal residence described in later sources for Hasmonean Jerusalem.

name: Alexandrium fortress
summary: Hasmonean/Herodian fortress traditionally identified with Sartaba overlooking the Jordan Valley.

name: Nazareth
summary: Galilean settlement identified with the hometown of Jesus in the Gospel traditions.

name: Sepphoris
summary: Major Galilean city near Nazareth, rebuilt under Herod Antipas and useful for regional historical context even though the Gospels do not name it.

name: Cana of Galilee
summary: The village named in John as the setting of the wedding sign and other episodes. Its modern identification is disputed.

name: Khirbet Qana
summary: Archaeological settlement in Lower Galilee proposed by many researchers as a candidate for Cana of Galilee.

name: Kafr Kanna
summary: Modern town associated in later Christian tradition with Cana of Galilee.

name: Capernaum
summary: Fishing and agricultural village on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee, a central setting in the Gospel ministry narratives.

name: Sea of Galilee
summary: Freshwater lake central to Jesus’ Galilean ministry and the fishing economy of the region.
aliases: Lake Gennesaret Sea of Tiberias Lake Kinneret

name: Bethsaida
summary: Village or town associated with several disciples and Gospel events near the Sea of Galilee. Its archaeological identification remains debated.

name: el-Araj
summary: Archaeological site near the Jordan inflow proposed as a candidate for New Testament Bethsaida.

name: et-Tell
summary: Large archaeological mound east of the Jordan inflow, long proposed as Bethsaida/Julias.

name: Chorazin
summary: Galilean settlement named with Bethsaida and Capernaum in the Gospel woes.

name: Magdala
summary: Important lakeside settlement on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, associated by name with Mary Magdalene.

name: Tiberias
summary: City founded by Herod Antipas on the western shore of the lake and named for Emperor Tiberius.
aliases: Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee

name: Plain of Gennesaret
summary: Fertile plain on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee, named in Gospel landing traditions.

name: Mount of Beatitudes — traditional area
summary: Traditional hillside commemorating the Sermon on the Mount north of the Sea of Galilee.

name: Tabgha — multiplication tradition
summary: Traditional Christian commemoration area for multiplication and post-resurrection traditions near the Sea of Galilee.

name: Country of the Gerasenes / Gadarenes
summary: Gospel region east of the Sea of Galilee associated with the healing of a possessed man; manuscript place-names and exact geography vary.

name: Gadara
summary: Major Decapolis city southeast of the Sea of Galilee, relevant to the “Gadarenes” textual tradition.

name: Kursi / east-shore candidate
summary: East-shore archaeological and pilgrimage site sometimes associated with the Gerasene/Gadarene episode.

name: Decapolis
summary: Loose regional grouping of Hellenistic-Roman cities east and southeast of Galilee, named in Gospel travel and crowd traditions.

name: Nain
summary: Galilean village associated in Luke with the raising of a widow’s son.

name: Sychar
summary: Samaritan place named in John 4 near Jacob’s well and Mount Gerizim. Its exact identification remains debated.

name: Askar — Sychar candidate
summary: Modern village northeast of Shechem proposed as the location of John’s Sychar.

name: Jacob’s Well
summary: Ancient well near Mount Gerizim traditionally identified with the well in John 4.

name: Bethany beyond the Jordan
summary: Place named in John for John the Baptist’s activity east of the Jordan; its exact location is disputed.

name: Al-Maghtas / Wadi al-Kharrar baptism landscape
summary: Archaeological and pilgrimage landscape on the east bank of the Jordan associated with the baptism of Jesus and Bethany beyond the Jordan.

name: Aenon near Salim
summary: Place of baptismal activity named in John 3. Its precise location remains uncertain.

name: Judean Wilderness
summary: Arid region east of Jerusalem and the Judean highlands associated with John the Baptist and Jesus’ temptation traditions.

name: Machaerus
summary: Herodian fortress east of the Dead Sea, identified by Josephus as the place where John the Baptist was imprisoned and executed.

name: Bethany
summary: Village on the eastern side of the Mount of Olives associated with Martha, Mary, Lazarus, and Jesus’ final visits to Jerusalem.

name: Bethphage
summary: Village on or near the Mount of Olives named in the approach to Jerusalem.

name: Gethsemane
summary: Place across the Kidron at the Mount of Olives where the Synoptic Gospels locate Jesus’ prayer and arrest.

name: Upper room of the Last Supper
summary: Unspecified furnished upper room in Jerusalem used in the Last Supper narratives.

name: Herod’s palace complex in Jerusalem
summary: Herodian royal complex on Jerusalem’s western hill, later relevant to debates over the Roman governor’s praetorium.

name: Antonia Fortress
summary: Fortified complex at the northwest corner of the Temple Mount, rebuilt and renamed by Herod the Great.

name: Pilate’s praetorium in Jerusalem
summary: The Roman governor’s headquarters named in the Passion narratives. Its precise Jerusalem location is debated.

name: Gabbatha / Lithostrotos
summary: Place-name associated in John with Pilate’s judgment seat.

name: Pool of Bethesda
summary: Pool complex north of the Temple Mount associated in John with a healing narrative.

name: Pool of Siloam — Second Temple period
summary: Large pool at the southern end of the City of David area associated in John 9 with the healing of the man born blind.

name: Golgotha
summary: Execution place outside Jerusalem associated with Jesus’ crucifixion. The exact spot is not independently recoverable.

name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre — Golgotha/Tomb tradition
summary: Longstanding Jerusalem site preserving the principal historical Christian identification of both Golgotha and Jesus’ tomb.

name: Garden Tomb
summary: Nineteenth-century Protestant alternative identification north of Jerusalem’s Old City.

name: Tomb of Jesus — textual location
summary: Burial place described in the Gospel narratives near the crucifixion location. Its exact modern identification remains a matter of historical argument and tradition.
aliases: New tomb of Joseph of Arimathea

name: Emmaus of Luke 24
summary: Village reached by two disciples from Jerusalem after the resurrection in Luke 24. Its identification is disputed.

name: el-Qubeibeh — Emmaus tradition
summary: Village northwest of Jerusalem identified in medieval Christian tradition with Luke’s Emmaus.

name: Arimathea
summary: Home town of Joseph of Arimathea. Its ancient location is not securely identified.

name: Mountain of the Transfiguration
summary: Unnamed high mountain in the Synoptic Transfiguration narratives.

name: Mount Hermon
summary: High mountain massif north of Galilee, relevant as a geographic candidate in discussions of the Transfiguration.

name: Unnamed mountain in Galilee (Matthew 28)
summary: Unnamed mountain in Galilee where Matthew places a resurrection appearance and commission.

name: Samaria (region)
summary: Broad Gospel-period regional anchor for Samaria, intentionally distinct from the ancient city of Samaria/Sebaste.

name: “Beautiful Gate” of the Jerusalem Temple
summary: Gate named in Acts 3 at which a man is healed. Which physical Temple gate the term designates is debated.

name: Solomon’s Portico / Colonnade
summary: Temple-complex portico named in Acts as a gathering location.

name: Akeldama / Field of Blood
summary: Jerusalem-area place associated in Acts 1 with the field connected to Judas.

name: Location of Stephen’s stoning
summary: Acts places Stephen’s execution outside the city but does not identify a recoverable gate or exact spot.

name: Lydda / Lod
summary: Judean plain city where Acts narrates Peter’s healing of Aeneas.

name: Azotus / Ashdod
summary: Coastal city named as Philip’s location after the encounter on the Gaza road.

name: Sharon Plain
summary: Coastal plain named in Acts 9 in connection with Lydda and the spread of the movement.

name: Antipatris
summary: Herodian/Roman city on the Jerusalem–Caesarea corridor where Paul’s military escort stops according to Acts 23.

name: Straight Street — Damascus
summary: Acts names the “street called Straight” in Damascus. A long east–west Roman street axis underlies the traditional identification.

name: House of Judas in Damascus
summary: House on Straight Street where Acts places Saul after the Damascus encounter.

name: Tarsus
summary: Major Cilician city identified by Acts as Paul’s birthplace and later location.

name: Syria and Cilicia corridor
summary: Broad regional corridor named in Acts 15 as Paul and Silas strengthen communities.

name: “Arabia” in Galatians 1
summary: Region Paul says he went to after his calling, before returning to Damascus. The territorial meaning is broad and the route is not described.

name: Cyprus
summary: Island crossed by Barnabas and Paul on the first missionary journey.

name: Salamis, Cyprus
summary: Major eastern Cypriot city where Acts says Barnabas and Paul proclaimed in Jewish synagogues.

name: Paphos
summary: Western Cypriot administrative center where Acts places the encounter with Sergius Paulus and Bar-Jesus/Elymas.

name: Perga
summary: Pamphylian city visited on the first missionary journey and again on the return.

name: Attalia
summary: Pamphylian port from which Paul and Barnabas sail back to Antioch according to Acts 14.

name: Antioch near Pisidia
summary: Roman-colony city in southern Galatia/Pisidia where Acts 13–14 narrates an extended synagogue and civic episode.

name: Iconium
summary: Central Anatolian city visited by Paul and Barnabas in Acts 14 and again in later journeys.

name: Lystra
summary: Lycaonian city associated with Paul’s first journey, the stoning episode, and Timothy’s home region.

name: Derbe
summary: Lycaonian city reached on the first missionary journey and revisited in Acts 16. The exact archaeological identification remains debated.

name: Kerti Höyük — Derbe candidate
summary: Major modern candidate for ancient Derbe.

name: Galatia — Pauline / Acts regional context
summary: Broad central-Anatolian context relevant to Acts and the addressees of Galatians. The identity of Paul’s “Galatians” in relation to provincial versus ethnic geography is debated.

name: Alexandria Troas
summary: Major Troad port city where Acts places Paul before crossing to Macedonia and again on the return journey.

name: Samothrace
summary: Aegean island named as an overnight point on the voyage from Troas to Neapolis.

name: Neapolis (Macedonia)
summary: Macedonian port of Philippi, generally identified with modern Kavala.

name: Philippi
summary: Roman colony in Macedonia where Acts narrates Lydia, imprisonment, and a new community.

name: Riverside prayer-place near Philippi
summary: Acts places the encounter with Lydia outside the city gate by a river or watercourse where prayer was customary.

name: Prison in Philippi — Acts narrative
summary: Acts narrates Paul and Silas imprisoned in Philippi, but no excavated building can be securely identified as that prison.

name: Amphipolis
summary: Macedonian city passed through on the route from Philippi toward Thessalonica.

name: Apollonia in Macedonia
summary: City on the Via Egnatia named between Amphipolis and Thessalonica in Acts 17.

name: Thessalonica
summary: Major Macedonian port and provincial center where Acts narrates synagogue preaching and opposition; recipient city of 1–2 Thessalonians.

name: Berea / Beroea
summary: Macedonian city where Acts praises receptive synagogue hearers before Paul travels toward Athens.

name: Athens
summary: Major Greek city where Acts narrates Paul engaging synagogue, marketplace, philosophers, and the Areopagus.

name: Areopagus — hill/council context
summary: Acts 17 says Paul was brought “to the Areopagus.” The term can refer to the council/body and, by extension, its setting; the exact speech spot is not certain.

name: Corinth
summary: Roman colony and Achaian center where Paul spends an extended period according to Acts and which receives major Pauline correspondence.

name: Bema in the Roman forum at Corinth
summary: Monumental speaking/judgment platform in Corinth’s forum, often discussed in relation to Gallio’s hearing of Paul.

name: Cenchreae
summary: Eastern port of Corinth named in Acts and Romans.

name: Achaia — Roman provincial context
summary: Roman province including Corinth and Athens in the first century CE.

name: Ephesus
summary: Major city of Roman Asia where Acts places Paul for an extended ministry and a major civic disturbance.

name: Great Theater of Ephesus
summary: Large theater associated with the civic assembly scene in Acts 19.

name: Hall of Tyrannus
summary: Lecture hall named in Acts 19 as a place where Paul reasoned daily in Ephesus.

name: Temple of Artemis at Ephesus
summary: Major sanctuary central to Ephesus’s identity and to the economic/religious context of Acts 19.

name: Asia — Roman provincial context
summary: Roman province of Asia, repeatedly named in Acts and Pauline correspondence.

name: Miletus
summary: Ionian port city where Acts 20 places Paul’s meeting with elders from Ephesus.

name: Assos
summary: Troad city where Acts says Paul joined his companions by ship after traveling overland.

name: Mitylene
summary: City on Lesbos named in Acts 20 as an overnight maritime stop.

name: Chios
summary: Aegean island named in Acts 20 as a sailing waypoint.

name: Samos
summary: Aegean island named in Acts 20 as a sailing waypoint.

name: Cos
summary: Island stop named in Acts 21 during Paul’s voyage toward Jerusalem.

name: Patara
summary: Lycian port where Paul’s party changes ships for the voyage toward Phoenicia.

name: Myra
summary: Lycian city/port region where the centurion transfers Paul to an Alexandrian grain ship bound west.

name: Cnidus
summary: Promontory/city region named in Acts 27 as the ship struggles westward before turning toward Crete.

name: Crete
summary: Large island along whose southern coast the Alexandrian ship sails in Acts 27.

name: Fair Havens, Crete
summary: Harbor named in Acts 27 near Lasea, generally identified with modern Kaloi Limenes.

name: Lasea
summary: Cretan city said to be near Fair Havens in Acts 27.

name: Phoenix / Phoenice, Crete
summary: Harbor the crew hoped to reach for winter in Acts 27. The exact harbor identification is debated.

name: Cauda / Clauda — Gavdos
summary: Island passed under for shelter during the storm in Acts 27, commonly identified with Gavdos.

name: Malta / Melite
summary: Island identified in Acts 28 after the shipwreck. Malta is the mainstream identification of Melite.

name: Exact shipwreck site on Malta
summary: Acts describes a bay with a beach but does not name a bay. Later traditions identify locations such as St Paul’s Bay.

name: Syracuse
summary: Sicilian city where Acts 28 says the voyage stopped for three days.

name: Rhegium
summary: Italian city at the Strait of Messina, a one-day stop on the voyage to Rome.

name: Puteoli
summary: Major Bay of Naples port where Acts says Paul stayed seven days with believers before continuing overland to Rome.

name: Forum of Appius / Appii Forum
summary: Station on the Via Appia where Roman believers meet Paul according to Acts 28.

name: Three Taverns
summary: Via Appia station where Acts says another group of believers met Paul.

name: Paul’s rented lodging in Rome
summary: Acts ends with Paul living under guard in rented quarters in Rome for two years.

name: Colossae
summary: Lycus Valley city addressed by Colossians and associated with Philemon’s network; Acts does not narrate a visit by Paul.

name: Laodicea on the Lycus
summary: Lycus Valley city mentioned in Colossians and later Revelation.

name: Hierapolis
summary: Lycus Valley city named in Colossians 4 alongside Laodicea and Colossae.

name: Illyricum in Romans 15
summary: Western Balkan region Paul names as the limit of his preaching “as far as Illyricum.” The phrase does not establish a specific city visit.

name: Phrygia — Acts regional context
summary: Broad inland Anatolian region named in Acts as part of Paul’s travel context. Its administrative/geographic extent varied across periods.

name: Macedonia — Acts regional context
summary: Roman provincial/regional context for repeated Pauline travel. Acts sometimes names Macedonia without listing every city visited.

name: Patmos
summary: Aegean island where the seer John says he was when he received the Revelation.

name: Cave of the Apocalypse — traditional site
summary: Later Christian tradition identifies this cave on Patmos with John’s visionary experience.

name: Smyrna
summary: Major port city of Roman Asia and the second of Revelation’s seven churches.

name: Pergamum
summary: Former Attalid capital and third church addressed in Revelation.

name: Great Altar of Pergamum
summary: Monumental Hellenistic altar from Pergamum, sometimes proposed as background to the phrase “Satan’s throne.”

name: Thyatira
summary: Commercial city of Lydia and fourth church addressed in Revelation.

name: Sardis
summary: Ancient Lydian capital and fifth church addressed in Revelation.

name: Philadelphia of Lydia
summary: Sixth church addressed in Revelation, located in the Lydian interior of Roman Asia.

name: Roman province of Asia — Revelation setting
summary: Broad provincial setting of the seven churches.

name: Babylon the Great — visionary city
summary: Revelation’s symbolic “Babylon” is a visionary city and political-religious image, not plotted as the archaeological city of Babylon.

name: Har-Magedon / Armageddon — visionary toponym
summary: Revelation 16:16 names Har-Magedon in an apocalyptic battle scene. Its etymology and relationship to historical Megiddo are debated.

name: Heavenly throne room — visionary space
summary: Revelation 4–5 describes a heavenly throne room with worship, living creatures, elders, and the Lamb.

name: The Abyss — visionary space
summary: Apocalyptic realm appearing in Revelation’s trumpet and beast imagery.

name: Gog and Magog — visionary nations
summary: Revelation 20 reuses Ezekiel’s Gog/Magog imagery for nations gathered from the earth after the millennium.

name: Lake of fire — visionary space
summary: Final-judgment image in Revelation 19–21.

name: New Jerusalem — visionary city
summary: Revelation 21–22 portrays a New Jerusalem descending from heaven, with immense symbolic dimensions, gates, foundations, river, and tree of life.
aliases: Holy City Jerusalem coming down out of heaven

name: River and tree of life — visionary landscape
summary: Revelation 22 reunites river, city, throne, and tree-of-life imagery in the final vision.
aliases: River of the water of life Tree of life

name: Adam
summary: The first human figure in the Genesis creation and Eden narratives.

name: Eve
summary: The first woman in the Genesis Eden narrative and mother figure in the early genealogies.

name: Noah
summary: Central figure of the flood narrative and post-flood genealogical transition.

name: Abraham
summary: Patriarch whose Genesis story moves from Mesopotamia through Haran into Canaan, Egypt, and the southern hill country.

name: Sarah
summary: Wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac; associated especially with Hebron/Machpelah in the burial narrative.

name: Lot
summary: Abraham’s nephew whose story is tied to the Jordan plain and the Sodom narrative.

name: Hagar
summary: Egyptian servant of Sarah and mother of Ishmael, associated with wilderness and well traditions.

name: Isaac
summary: Son of Abraham and Sarah; his narrative is centered mainly in the southern Canaan/Negev zone.

name: Rebekah
summary: Wife of Isaac, brought from Abraham’s wider kin network in upper Mesopotamia.

name: Jacob
summary: Son of Isaac whose journeys link Beersheba, Bethel, Haran/Paddan-aram, Gilead, the Jabbok, Shechem, and Hebron.

name: Esau
summary: Brother of Jacob and ancestral figure associated in Genesis with Seir/Edom.

name: Rachel
summary: Wife of Jacob and mother of Joseph and Benjamin; part of the Haran-to-Canaan return narrative.

name: Leah
summary: Wife of Jacob and mother of several sons who become ancestral tribal figures in Genesis.

name: Joseph
summary: Son of Jacob whose story moves from the hill country through Dothan to Egypt, where he rises to power and receives his family.

name: Judah
summary: Son of Jacob who becomes prominent in the Joseph cycle and the family’s move to Egypt.

name: Moses
summary: Central leader of the Exodus and wilderness narratives, associated with Egypt, Sinai/Horeb, Kadesh, and the plains of Moab. The identity of the Pharaoh(s) in his story is not named by the biblical text.
scripture: Exodus 2 Exodus 3 Exodus 12 Exodus 19 Numbers 20 Deuteronomy 34

name: Aaron
summary: Brother of Moses and first high priest in the Pentateuchal narrative, present through the Exodus, Sinai, and wilderness episodes.

name: Miriam
summary: Sister of Moses and Aaron, associated with the sea song and the Hazeroth episode.

name: Pharaoh of the Exodus
summary: The ruler opposed by Moses in Exodus is never named in the biblical text. Attempts to identify him with a specific New Kingdom pharaoh depend on chronological models and remain disputed.

name: Joshua
summary: Successor to Moses in the biblical narrative, leading the Jordan crossing and campaigns in Joshua before receiving Timnath-serah.

name: Caleb
summary: One of the spies who supports entering the land and later receives Hebron in the Judah traditions.

name: Rahab
summary: A woman of Jericho who shelters Israelite spies in Joshua 2 and is spared in the city’s fall narrative.

name: Balak
summary: King of Moab in Numbers who summons Balaam as Israel camps east of the Jordan.

name: Balaam
summary: Non-Israelite diviner in Numbers whose oracles are set in Moab. Separate ancient inscriptional evidence from Deir ʿAlla mentions a seer named Balaam son of Beor, but its relationship to the biblical figure is interpretive.

name: Deborah
summary: Prophet and judge who summons Barak and celebrates victory over Sisera in Judges 4–5.

name: Barak
summary: Commander from Kedesh in Naphtali who leads forces from Mount Tabor against Sisera.

name: Sisera
summary: Commander of Jabin’s army in Judges 4, associated with Harosheth-hagoyim and the Kishon battle.

name: Jael
summary: Woman who kills Sisera after the battle in Judges 4; the precise location of Heber the Kenite’s encampment is not securely mapped.

name: Gideon
summary: Judge from Ophrah of the Abiezrites who fights Midian after assembling at the Spring of Harod.

name: Jephthah
summary: Gileadite leader whose conflict with Ammon is narrated in Judges 10–12. His home and Mizpah setting cannot be mapped precisely.

name: Samson
summary: Judge whose stories unfold along the Judah–Philistia frontier, especially Zorah, Timnah, the Sorek Valley, and Gaza.

name: Delilah
summary: Woman of the Sorek Valley in Judges 16 whose precise home is unknown.

name: Othniel
summary: The first judge named in Judges 3 and, in Judges 1, the warrior associated with the capture of Debir/Kiriath-sepher.

name: Ehud
summary: Benjaminite judge who kills Eglon of Moab and rallies Israel from the Ephraimite hill country in Judges 3.

name: Eglon
summary: King of Moab in the Ehud narrative. Judges associates his control with the City of Palms/Jericho region.

name: Abimelech
summary: Son of Gideon whose kingship and violent conflict center on Shechem before his death at Thebez.

name: Micah of the Hill Country
summary: A man from the hill country of Ephraim whose household shrine becomes part of the Danite migration narrative in Judges 17–18.

name: The Levite of Judges 19
summary: An unnamed Levite from the hill country of Ephraim whose journey from Bethlehem to Gibeah precipitates the civil-war narrative of Judges 19–21.

name: Ruth
summary: A Moabite woman whose migration with Naomi to Bethlehem forms the geographic frame of Ruth and whose genealogy leads to David.

name: Naomi
summary: A Bethlehemite woman who returns from Moab with Ruth after family loss.

name: Boaz
summary: A Bethlehem landholder and kinsman-redeemer in the Ruth narrative.

name: Eli
summary: Priest at Shiloh whose household frames Samuel’s early sanctuary narrative and the ark crisis.

name: Samuel
summary: Prophet, judge, and kingmaker whose narratives move between Shiloh, Ramah, Mizpah, Gilgal, Bethlehem, and Saul’s court world.

name: Saul
summary: The first king in Samuel’s narrative, associated with Benjamin, Gibeah, Philistine warfare, and the final campaign at Gilboa.

name: Jonathan
summary: Saul’s son and David’s ally, active in the Philistine conflict and killed with Saul on Mount Gilboa.

name: David
summary: Bethlehemite warrior, fugitive, king at Hebron, and ruler centered on Jerusalem. His narratives span the Shephelah, Judean wilderness, Philistine cities, Transjordan, and Jerusalem.
scripture: 1 Samuel 16 1 Samuel 17 2 Samuel 2 2 Samuel 5 2 Samuel 6 2 Samuel 15 2 Samuel 24

name: Goliath
summary: The Philistine champion from Gath in the Elah Valley narrative.

name: Michal
summary: Saul’s daughter and David’s wife, associated especially with Gibeah and later Jerusalem narratives.

name: Abigail
summary: A woman associated with Carmel and Maon who intervenes between David and Nabal and later becomes David’s wife.

name: Abner
summary: Saul’s military commander and later supporter of Ish-bosheth during the civil conflict before David controls all Israel.

name: Joab
summary: David’s principal commander, active at Gibeon, Jerusalem, Rabbah, and during Absalom’s revolt.

name: Ish-bosheth
summary: A son of Saul installed as king over much of Israel from Mahanaim while David reigns at Hebron.

name: Bathsheba
summary: A central figure in the David and Solomon succession narratives in Jerusalem.

name: Nathan the Prophet
summary: Court prophet in Jerusalem who delivers the dynastic oracle and later supports Solomon’s accession.

name: Absalom
summary: David’s son whose rebellion drives the king from Jerusalem across the Kidron and toward Transjordan before the conflict near Mahanaim.

name: Solomon
summary: David’s successor, associated with Gihon, Gibeon, temple construction, royal building, Phoenician exchange, and Red Sea trade traditions.
scripture: 1 Kings 1 1 Kings 3 1 Kings 5 1 Kings 6 1 Kings 8 1 Kings 9 1 Kings 10

name: Hiram of Tyre
summary: Phoenician ruler associated in the biblical narratives with timber, craftsmen, and maritime exchange with David and Solomon.

name: Queen of Sheba
summary: A royal visitor in 1 Kings 10 and 2 Chronicles 9. The text connects her with Sheba; no independent itinerary or palace can be mapped with confidence.

name: Rehoboam
summary: Son of Solomon and king in Jerusalem when the northern tribes reject his rule at Shechem.

name: Jeroboam I
summary: First king of the Northern Kingdom in the Kings narrative; associated with Shechem, Penuel, Bethel, and Dan.

name: Shoshenq I
summary: Egyptian pharaoh commonly identified with the biblical Shishak who campaigns in the Levant during Rehoboam’s reign.

name: Omri
summary: Northern king who founds Samaria and establishes the dynasty later labeled “house of Omri” in foreign sources.

name: Ahab
summary: Son of Omri; associated with Samaria, Jezreel, conflicts with Aram, Elijah, and—outside Kings—the coalition at Qarqar.

name: Jezebel
summary: Phoenician royal woman, wife of Ahab, central to the Elijah cycle and the Naboth/Jehu narratives.

name: Elijah
summary: Prophet whose stories move between Gilead, Phoenicia, Carmel, Jezreel, Beersheba, and Horeb/Sinai.

name: Elisha
summary: Successor to Elijah whose narratives center on the Jordan, Samaria, Dothan, Shunem, and Israel-Aram relations.

name: Naaman
summary: Aramean commander in 2 Kings 5 who seeks healing through Elisha and washes in the Jordan.

name: Mesha of Moab
summary: Moabite king known from both 2 Kings 3 and the Mesha Stele, though the texts present different episodes and perspectives.

name: Jehoshaphat
summary: King of Judah who appears as Ahab’s ally at Ramoth-gilead and joins the Moab campaign in 2 Kings 3.

name: Jehu
summary: Army commander anointed king during the Ramoth-gilead crisis; his coup reaches Jezreel and Samaria. Assyrian evidence records tribute from Jehu.

name: Hazael
summary: King of Aram-Damascus and major opponent of Israel and Judah. A damaged Aramaic victory inscription from Tel Dan is often connected with his reign, though attribution is debated.

name: Athaliah
summary: Royal woman who seizes power in Judah after Ahaziah’s death before being overthrown in the Joash narrative.

name: Joash of Judah
summary: King of Judah associated with Temple repairs and Hazael’s pressure on Jerusalem.

name: Amos
summary: Prophet from Tekoa whose oracles address Israel and its neighbors; Amos 7 places a confrontation at the royal sanctuary of Bethel.

name: Jeroboam II
summary: Northern king during a period of territorial recovery and prosperity that forms part of the setting for Amos and Hosea.

name: Hosea
summary: Prophet whose book addresses the Northern Kingdom in the final decades before Assyrian conquest, using Israel/Ephraim/Samaria as major political-theological terms.

name: Jonah
summary: A prophet named Jonah son of Amittai appears in 2 Kings 14; the book of Jonah places its narrative between Joppa, the sea, and Nineveh. The book’s composition and historicity are separate scholarly questions.

name: Ahaz
summary: King of Judah during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis who appeals to Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria.

name: Pekah
summary: King of Israel who allies with Rezin of Damascus against Judah before Assyrian intervention.

name: Hoshea
summary: Last king of the Northern Kingdom in Kings; his revolt against Assyria precedes the siege and fall of Samaria.

name: Isaiah
summary: Jerusalem-centered prophet active through the Assyrian crises of Ahaz and Hezekiah; his book preserves detailed Jerusalem and imperial geography.

name: Micah
summary: Prophet associated with Moresheth in the Shephelah whose oracles address Samaria and Jerusalem amid Assyrian pressure.

name: Tiglath-pileser III
summary: Assyrian king whose western campaigns transformed Syria-Palestine, annexing Damascus and northern Israelite territories and receiving tribute from regional rulers.

name: Shalmaneser III
summary: Assyrian king whose inscriptions record Qarqar and later tribute from Jehu.

name: Shalmaneser V
summary: Assyrian king named in Kings as beginning the siege of Samaria; his short reign complicates attribution of the city’s final capture.

name: Sargon II
summary: Successor of Shalmaneser V whose inscriptions claim the conquest and deportation of Samaria and who later builds Dur-Sharrukin.

name: Hezekiah
summary: King of Judah during the 701 BCE Assyrian campaign, associated in biblical tradition with reform, Jerusalem waterworks, and resistance to Sennacherib.

name: Sennacherib
summary: Assyrian king whose 701 BCE campaign devastated Judah and captured Lachish; his inscriptions describe Hezekiah confined in Jerusalem but do not claim Jerusalem’s capture.

name: Necho II
summary: Egyptian pharaoh whose northward campaign forms the setting for Josiah’s death at Megiddo and the struggle over Syria-Palestine.

name: Josiah
summary: King of Judah associated with centralizing reforms and killed after confronting/meeting Pharaoh Necho II at Megiddo.

name: Jehoahaz of Judah
summary: Son of Josiah briefly installed as king before Necho II deposes him and takes him to Egypt.

name: Jehoiakim
summary: King installed by Necho II who later becomes subject to Babylon and rebels, placing Judah between Egyptian and Babylonian power.

name: Jehoiachin
summary: Young Judean king deported to Babylon in 597 BCE; Babylonian administrative tablets later name Yaukin, king of Judah, and his household.

name: Zedekiah
summary: King installed by Nebuchadnezzar II whose rebellion ends with Jerusalem’s destruction and his capture near Jericho before judgment at Riblah.

name: Jeremiah
summary: Prophet from Anathoth whose book spans Josiah through the fall of Jerusalem and the refugee movement into Egypt.

name: Baruch son of Neriah
summary: Scribe associated with Jeremiah, especially the scroll narrative of Jeremiah 36.

name: Nebuchadnezzar II
summary: Babylonian king whose reign includes the 597 capture of Jerusalem and the later destruction of the city/temple; also the dominant royal figure in Daniel 1–4.

name: Gedaliah son of Ahikam
summary: Appointed over the population remaining in Judah after Jerusalem’s fall and based at Mizpah; assassinated soon afterward in the biblical narrative.

name: Ishmael son of Nethaniah
summary: Figure who kills Gedaliah at Mizpah according to Kings and Jeremiah.

name: Johanan son of Kareah
summary: Military leader who opposes Ishmael and then leads the surviving group into Egypt, taking Jeremiah and Baruch.

name: Ezekiel
summary: Priest-prophet whose book dates visions among the exiles by the Kebar in Babylonia while repeatedly envisioning Jerusalem.

name: Daniel
summary: Principal figure of Daniel, whose court tales and visions are set in Babylonian and Persian imperial worlds.

name: Hananiah
summary: Companion of Daniel given the Babylonian court name Shadrach in Daniel 1.

name: Mishael
summary: Companion of Daniel given the Babylonian court name Meshach.

name: Azariah
summary: Companion of Daniel given the Babylonian court name Abednego.

name: Belshazzar
summary: Historically attested son of Nabonidus who exercised royal authority in Babylonia; Daniel 5 calls him king and sets the banquet narrative under him.

name: Nabonidus
summary: Last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire; father of Belshazzar and ruler when Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BCE.

name: Darius the Mede
summary: Ruler named in Daniel after the fall of Babylon. No independently identified historical monarch under this exact title/person has achieved consensus.

name: Cyrus II
summary: Founder of the Achaemenid Empire who conquered Babylon in 539 BCE; Ezra credits him with authorizing restoration of the Jerusalem temple.

name: Sheshbazzar
summary: Figure called prince/governor of Judah in Ezra and associated with returning temple vessels/foundation tradition; relationship to Zerubbabel remains debated.

name: Zerubbabel
summary: Davidic-descended governor/leader associated with the return community and rebuilding of the temple.

name: Jeshua / Joshua son of Jozadak
summary: High-priestly leader associated with Zerubbabel in altar and temple restoration traditions.

name: Darius I
summary: Persian king under whom Ezra dates the completion of the Jerusalem temple; his empire is independently illuminated by Behistun and extensive Achaemenid evidence.

name: Haggai
summary: Prophet whose dated oracles urge Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the community to rebuild the temple.

name: Zechariah
summary: Prophet whose visions and oracles are dated in the reign of Darius and center on Jerusalem’s restoration.

name: Ahasuerus
summary: King in Esther, commonly identified with Xerxes I because the Hebrew name corresponds closely to Old Persian Khshayarsha; the narrative’s individual events are not independently documented.

name: Esther
summary: Jewish heroine of Esther who becomes queen in the Susa court narrative.

name: Mordecai
summary: Jewish court figure and guardian/relative of Esther in the narrative.

name: Haman
summary: Royal official and antagonist in Esther’s narrative.

name: Artaxerxes I
summary: Persian king conventionally identified as the Artaxerxes of Nehemiah and commonly of Ezra 7, though Ezra’s absolute chronology has been debated.

name: Ezra
summary: Priest-scribe who leads a group from Babylonia to Jerusalem in Ezra 7–8 and is associated with Torah teaching/reform.

name: Nehemiah
summary: Cupbearer in the Susa court narrative who becomes governor in Judah and leads Jerusalem wall reconstruction.

name: Sanballat the Horonite
summary: Opponent of Nehemiah in the wall narrative; the name also appears in the Persian-period Samarian milieu known from external evidence, though person-by-person correlations require care.

name: Tobiah
summary: Official/elite opponent of Nehemiah in the biblical narrative, linked with Ammonite identity and Jerusalem networks.

name: Geshem the Arab
