summary: Arabian figure named among Nehemiah’s opponents; broader Arabian political connections are historical context, but exact office and territory are debated.

name: Manasseh of Judah
summary: Long-reigning king of Judah after Hezekiah. Assyrian royal texts independently name Manasseh king of Judah among western vassal rulers.

name: Amon of Judah
summary: Son and successor of Manasseh whose short reign ends in assassination before Josiah becomes king.

name: Zephaniah
summary: Prophet dated by the book to the reign of Josiah; his oracles range from Jerusalem/Judah to Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria/Nineveh.

name: Nahum
summary: Prophet whose book is an oracle concerning Nineveh and evokes the fall of Thebes/No-Amon as a historical analogy.

name: Habakkuk
summary: Prophet whose dialogue names the Chaldeans/Babylonians as a rising military power. The book’s exact date within that transition is debated.

name: Obadiah
summary: Prophetic voice against Edom focused on violence against Jerusalem. The date—often linked to a destruction of Jerusalem—is debated.

name: Alexander III of Macedon
summary: Macedonian king whose conquest ended Achaemenid rule across the Levant and Egypt and created the geopolitical framework of the Hellenistic age.

name: Ptolemy I Soter
summary: Alexander’s general who established Ptolemaic rule in Egypt and contested Coele-Syria/Judea during the Successor wars.

name: Ptolemy II Philadelphus
summary: Ptolemaic king associated by later tradition with the Greek translation of the Torah; the historical translation process was likely more complex than the idealized Letter of Aristeas account.

name: Seleucus I Nicator
summary: Founder of the Seleucid dynasty and of major royal cities including Antioch and Seleucia Pieria.

name: Antiochus III the Great
summary: Seleucid king whose victory over Ptolemaic forces at Panium around 200 BCE brought Coele-Syria and Judea under Seleucid control.

name: Seleucus IV Philopator
summary: Seleucid king preceding Antiochus IV; administrative evidence from his reign illuminates royal oversight of temples in Coele-Syria/Phoenicia.

name: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
summary: Seleucid king whose interventions in Jerusalem and restrictive decrees stand at the center of 1–2 Maccabees and the Maccabean revolt.

name: Onias III
summary: Jerusalem high priest deposed during the political crisis preceding the Maccabean revolt.

name: Onias IV
summary: A later Oniad priest associated by Josephus with the foundation of a Jewish temple in Egypt, usually connected with Leontopolis. Josephus’s Onias genealogy and chronology require careful source criticism.

name: Jason
summary: High-priestly claimant associated in 2 Maccabees with a program of Hellenizing civic institutions in Jerusalem.

name: Menelaus
summary: High priest installed amid the political struggles of Antiochus IV’s reign; ancient sources portray him polemically and details require source criticism.

name: Mattathias
summary: Priestly patriarch associated by 1 Maccabees with Modein and the beginning of armed resistance to Seleucid decrees.

name: Judas Maccabeus
summary: Military leader of the revolt associated with victories at Emmaus and Beth-zur and the rededication of the Jerusalem temple in 164 BCE.

name: Jonathan Apphus
summary: Brother of Judas who became leader and high priest amid shifting Seleucid alliances.

name: Simon Thassi
summary: Brother of Judas and Jonathan whose rule is associated with effective Judean independence and removal of the Seleucid garrison from Jerusalem.

name: John Hyrcanus I
summary: Hasmonean high priest and ruler associated with territorial expansion into Idumea and Samaria and the destruction of the Mount Gerizim sanctuary.

name: Aristobulus I
summary: Hasmonean ruler commonly regarded as the first of the dynasty to take the title of king, ruling briefly in 104/103 BCE.

name: Alexander Jannaeus
summary: Hasmonean king and high priest whose long reign combined expansion, coastal warfare and severe internal conflict.

name: Salome Alexandra
summary: Hasmonean queen whose reign (76–67 BCE in conventional chronology) followed Alexander Jannaeus and preceded the civil conflict of her sons.

name: Hyrcanus II
summary: Hasmonean high priest and claimant whose rivalry with Aristobulus II drew Pompey into Judean politics.

name: Aristobulus II
summary: Hasmonean king and rival of Hyrcanus II, defeated during Pompey’s intervention.

name: Pompey the Great
summary: Roman commander who reorganized the eastern Mediterranean and captured Jerusalem in 63 BCE during the Hasmonean civil war.

name: Antipater the Idumaean
summary: Idumaean political leader and father of Herod who became a central intermediary in Judean politics under Hyrcanus II and Rome.

name: Julius Caesar
summary: Roman dictator whose eastern settlements strengthened Hyrcanus II and Antipater after the Alexandrian War.

name: Antigonus II Mattathias
summary: Last Hasmonean king, installed amid Parthian intervention in 40 BCE and defeated when Herod captured Jerusalem in 37 BCE.

name: Herod the Great
summary: Roman client king who captured Jerusalem in 37 BCE and transformed Judea through extensive building, administrative and dynastic programs.

name: Mark Antony
summary: Roman triumvir whose eastern patronage shaped Herod’s rise before Antony’s defeat by Octavian.

name: Cleopatra VII
summary: Last Ptolemaic queen, allied with Antony and an important regional rival/neighbor in Herod’s political world.

name: Octavian / Augustus
summary: Victor at Actium and first Roman emperor; confirmed Herod after Antony’s defeat and became the imperial ruler named in Luke’s birth narrative.

name: Nicanor
summary: Seleucid commander defeated and killed by Judas Maccabeus in the campaign associated with Adasa.

name: Bacchides
summary: Seleucid commander who defeated Judas at Elasa and later fought Jonathan’s movement.

name: Jesus of Nazareth
summary: Central figure of the four Gospels. The atlas maps textual movements and first-century settings while keeping theological claims, exact chronology, and disputed site identifications distinct from geographic evidence.

name: Mary, mother of Jesus
summary: Mother of Jesus in the Gospel infancy narratives and later scenes.

name: Joseph
summary: Joseph, husband of Mary, appears in Matthew and Luke’s infancy narratives and is associated with Bethlehem, Egypt, and Nazareth.

name: John the Baptist
summary: Jewish prophetic and baptismal figure active in the Jordan region; executed under Herod Antipas. Josephus independently discusses John and associates his imprisonment with Machaerus.
scripture: Matthew 3:1–17 Mark 1:2–11 Luke 3:1–22 John 1:19–34 Josephus, Antiquities 18.116–119

name: Zechariah
summary: Priest in Luke’s infancy narrative and father of John the Baptist.

name: Elizabeth
summary: Relative of Mary and mother of John the Baptist in Luke’s infancy narrative.

name: Herod Antipas
summary: Son of Herod the Great and tetrarch of Galilee and Perea; central political figure in the John the Baptist narratives and Luke’s Passion account.

name: Herod Archelaus
summary: Son of Herod the Great who ruled Judea, Samaria, and Idumea as ethnarch until deposition by Rome.

name: Philip the Tetrarch
summary: Son of Herod the Great who ruled territories northeast of Galilee and developed Paneas/Caesarea Philippi.

name: Tiberius Caesar
summary: Roman emperor during the public ministries of John the Baptist and Jesus.

name: Publius Sulpicius Quirinius
summary: Roman official associated by Josephus with the census of Judea in 6 CE and by Luke with the birth narrative; reconciling the chronological references is a major historical problem.

name: Pontius Pilate
summary: Roman prefect of Judea under Tiberius. Independently attested by inscription and ancient literary sources; the exact Jerusalem praetorium used during Jesus’ trial is debated.
scripture: Matthew 27 Mark 15 Luke 23 John 18:28–40 Pilate inscription, Caesarea Tacitus, Annals 15.44

name: Joseph Caiaphas
summary: Jerusalem high priest under Roman rule, named in Gospel Passion narratives and Josephus. An ossuary inscription is often associated with his family but is not absolute proof of identity.

name: Annas
summary: Former high priest and influential priestly patriarch, named in Luke and John.

name: Peter
summary: Galilean disciple prominently associated with Capernaum, the Sea of Galilee, Caesarea Philippi narratives, and Jerusalem.

name: Andrew
summary: Disciple and brother of Peter, associated with Bethsaida and Galilee.

name: James son of Zebedee
summary: Galilean disciple, brother of John, associated with the fishing narratives and Transfiguration.

name: John son of Zebedee
summary: Galilean disciple, brother of James, prominent in Synoptic disciple lists and later Christian tradition.

name: Philip
summary: Disciple associated especially with Bethsaida and the Johannine narratives.

name: Nathanael
summary: Disciple in John associated with Cana of Galilee.

name: Matthew
summary: Disciple and tax collector in Gospel tradition, associated with Jesus’ Galilean ministry.

name: Thomas
summary: Disciple prominent in John, including the Jerusalem and Galilee resurrection narratives.

name: Mary Magdalene
summary: Follower of Jesus named in crucifixion, burial, and resurrection traditions; her epithet links her to Magdala.

name: Martha
summary: Woman associated with Bethany, Mary, and Lazarus in Luke and John.

name: Mary of Bethany
summary: Sister of Martha and Lazarus in John, associated with Bethany and the anointing narrative.

name: Lazarus of Bethany
summary: Man of Bethany raised by Jesus in John’s narrative and brother of Martha and Mary.

name: Nicodemus
summary: Jerusalem figure in John, appearing in a nighttime dialogue, a council scene, and Jesus’ burial.

name: Joseph of Arimathea
summary: Figure in all four Gospel burial narratives who provides or arranges Jesus’ tomb.

name: Zacchaeus
summary: Chief tax collector encountered by Jesus at Jericho in Luke.

name: Simon of Cyrene
summary: Man compelled to carry Jesus’ cross in the Synoptic Passion narratives; his origin is Cyrene, but the encounter occurs in Jerusalem.

name: Barabbas
summary: Prisoner released in the Passion narratives instead of Jesus.

name: Jairus
summary: Synagogue leader in the Galilean healing narrative of Jairus’s daughter.

name: Judas Iscariot
summary: Disciple associated with betrayal and Jesus’ arrest in the Passion narratives.

name: Herodias
summary: Herodian princess whose marriage to Herod Antipas is central to the Gospel account of John the Baptist’s execution.

name: Paul / Saul of Tarsus
summary: Apostle and missionary central to Acts 9–28 and author of the undisputed Pauline letters. The atlas distinguishes Acts’ narrative chronology from Paul’s own letters where correlations are debated.

name: Matthias
summary: Disciple chosen in Acts 1 to replace Judas among the Twelve.

name: Stephen
summary: Hellenistic Jewish member of the Jerusalem community whose speech and execution dominate Acts 6–7.

name: Philip the Evangelist
summary: One of the Seven in Acts, associated with Samaria, the Gaza road, Azotus, and later Caesarea.

name: Barnabas
summary: Cypriot Jewish follower of Jesus and major partner of Paul in Antioch and the first missionary journey.

name: Ananias of Damascus
summary: Disciple in Damascus who visits Saul in Acts 9.

name: Cornelius
summary: Roman centurion at Caesarea whose household forms a pivotal episode in Acts 10.

name: Tabitha / Dorcas
summary: Disciple at Joppa raised in the Acts narrative after Peter is summoned from Lydda.

name: Agabus
summary: Prophet in Acts associated with a famine prediction at Antioch and later with Paul’s impending arrest at Caesarea.

name: Herod Agrippa I
summary: Herodian ruler who receives Judea and Samaria under Claudius; Acts 12 associates him with James’s execution, Peter’s imprisonment, and his own death at Caesarea.

name: James, brother of Jesus
summary: Prominent Jerusalem leader in Acts 12, 15, and 21 and in Paul’s letters.

name: John Mark
summary: Jerusalem-linked associate of Barnabas and Paul who accompanies part of the first journey.

name: Sergius Paulus
summary: Proconsul of Cyprus named in Acts 13 at Paphos.

name: Bar-Jesus / Elymas
summary: Jewish magician/prophet in Acts 13 associated with the Paphos episode.

name: Silas / Silvanus
summary: Jerusalem delegate and missionary companion of Paul on the second journey.

name: Timothy
summary: Pauline coworker from the Lystra/Derbe region who joins the journey in Acts 16 and appears in several letters.

name: Lydia
summary: Purple-cloth dealer from Thyatira encountered at Philippi in Acts 16.

name: Jason of Thessalonica
summary: Host associated with Paul and Silas in the Thessalonian disturbance of Acts 17.

name: Dionysius the Areopagite
summary: Athenian hearer named among those who joined Paul after the Areopagus speech.

name: Damaris
summary: Woman named in Acts 17 among those who believed after Paul’s Athenian address.

name: Priscilla / Prisca
summary: Jewish Christian coworker of Paul and Aquila, associated with Corinth, Ephesus, and Rome.

name: Aquila
summary: Jewish Christian coworker of Priscilla and Paul, originally of Pontus and associated with Rome, Corinth, and Ephesus.

name: Claudius
summary: Roman emperor (41–54 CE), relevant to Agrippa I, the Judean famine context, and Acts 18’s notice of Jews leaving Rome.

name: Lucius Junius Gallio Annaeanus
summary: Roman proconsul of Achaia before whom Acts places a case against Paul in Corinth.

name: Crispus
summary: Synagogue leader in Corinth named in Acts 18 and 1 Corinthians 1.

name: Sosthenes
summary: Synagogue leader named in Acts 18; a Sosthenes also appears in 1 Corinthians 1:1, but identity is not assumed as certain.

name: Apollos
summary: Alexandrian Jewish teacher active in Ephesus and Corinth in Acts 18–19 and 1 Corinthians.

name: Demetrius of Ephesus
summary: Silversmith named in Acts 19 as an organizer of the disturbance connected with Artemis-related craft.

name: Tyrannus
summary: Person associated with the lecture hall used by Paul in Acts 19.

name: Eutychus
summary: Young man in the Troas narrative of Acts 20.

name: Trophimus the Ephesian
summary: Pauline companion from Asia whose presence becomes part of the accusation leading to Paul’s Jerusalem arrest.

name: Claudius Lysias
summary: Roman tribune in Jerusalem who arrests/protects Paul and transfers him toward Caesarea.

name: Ananias son of Nedebaios
summary: Jerusalem high priest who appears in Acts 23–24 and is also known from Josephus.

name: Antonius Felix
summary: Roman procurator of Judea before whom Paul is held and heard at Caesarea.

name: Drusilla
summary: Jewish wife of Felix who appears with him in Acts 24.

name: Porcius Festus
summary: Roman procurator who succeeds Felix and hears Paul’s case at Caesarea.

name: Herod Agrippa II
summary: Herodian ruler who hears Paul with Bernice at Caesarea in Acts 25–26.

name: Berenice
summary: Sister of Agrippa II who appears with him in Caesarea during Paul’s hearing.

name: Julius the centurion
summary: Centurion of the Augustan cohort charged with transporting Paul toward Rome in Acts 27.

name: Aristarchus of Thessalonica
summary: Macedonian companion of Paul named in Acts 19, 20, and the voyage narrative.

name: Publius of Malta
summary: Leading man of the island named in Acts 28 who receives Paul’s party.

name: Epaphras
summary: Coworker associated with Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis in Colossians.

name: Philemon
summary: Recipient of the letter to Philemon, associated by the letter’s network with the Colossian context.

name: Onesimus
summary: Figure central to Philemon and named in Colossians 4:9.

name: Titus
summary: Pauline coworker prominent in Galatians and 2 Corinthians; he is not named in Acts.

name: John of Patmos
summary: The named seer and authorial voice of Revelation. Traditional Christianity often identified him with John son of Zebedee, but the project keeps the identities separate because authorship is debated.
aliases: John the seer John of Revelation

name: Domitian
summary: Roman emperor under whom later Christian tradition commonly places Revelation’s composition. The book itself does not name Domitian, and its date remains debated.

name: Antipas of Pergamum
summary: Named in Revelation 2:13 as a faithful witness killed where the church of Pergamum lived. Later martyr traditions add details not present in Revelation.

name: “Jezebel” of Thyatira
summary: Woman or symbolic/polemical designation in Revelation 2:20–23. She is not the ninth-century BCE queen Jezebel and is modeled separately.

name: Michael
summary: Heavenly warrior who battles the dragon in Revelation 12.

name: Eden narrative
summary: Genesis situates the first human pair in a divinely planted garden associated with four rivers. The atlas leaves Eden unpinned because a recoverable modern location is not established.

name: Ark rests in the mountains of Ararat
summary: Genesis describes the ark resting in the “mountains of Ararat.”

name: Babel and the tower
summary: The Babel narrative is set in Shinar and explains linguistic dispersion in theological/literary terms.

name: Abram leaves Haran for Canaan
summary: Genesis describes Abram departing Haran and traveling into Canaan.

name: Abram goes down to Egypt
summary: A famine prompts Abram to travel from Canaan toward Egypt and later return.

name: Abram and Melchizedek
summary: After the kings narrative, Melchizedek king of Salem blesses Abram.

name: Sodom and Gomorrah narrative
summary: Genesis 18–19 describes judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah and Lot’s escape toward Zoar.

name: Binding of Isaac / Akedah
summary: Genesis 22 narrates Abraham traveling to the land of Moriah with Isaac.

name: Jacob’s dream at Bethel
summary: On the way from Beersheba toward Haran, Jacob names the place Bethel after his dream.

name: Jacob wrestles near the Jabbok
summary: Jacob crosses the Jabbok and receives the name Israel in the Peniel narrative.

name: Joseph sold near Dothan
summary: Joseph’s brothers encounter him near Dothan; merchants carry him toward Egypt.

name: Jacob’s household moves to Egypt
summary: After stopping at Beersheba, Jacob’s household travels to Egypt and is settled in Goshen.

name: Forced labor and the store cities
summary: Exodus associates Israelite forced labor with Pithom and Rameses. Pi-Ramesses is archaeologically known; Pithom remains disputed and the labor episode itself is not an excavated event marker.

name: Departure from Rameses
summary: The narrative sequence moves from Rameses to Succoth and onward toward the wilderness. The exact road and stations after Rameses are not securely identified.

name: Crossing of the sea
summary: Exodus 14–15 describes escape through the sea and the defeat of Pharaoh’s force. The water body and crossing point remain geographically unresolved.

name: Covenant at Sinai
summary: Exodus places Israel at Mount Sinai/Horeb for covenant, law, and sanctuary traditions. The mountain’s modern location is unknown.

name: Golden calf episode
summary: The golden calf narrative occurs at the Sinai camp while Moses is on the mountain. It is a textual event without an archaeologically identifiable camp location.

name: The spies and Kadesh-barnea
summary: Numbers sends spies from the wilderness and later locates the congregation at Kadesh. ʿAin el-Qudeirat is the leading site identification for Kadesh-barnea.

name: Death of Aaron at Mount Hor
summary: Numbers places Aaron’s death at Mount Hor. Jabal Harun is a later traditional candidate, not a proven biblical location.

name: Conflict with Sihon and Heshbon
summary: Numbers and Deuteronomy narrate Israel’s defeat of Sihon and occupation of territory centered on Heshbon. Tell Hesban is the standard geographic candidate for Heshbon, but its archaeological chronology is debated.

name: Balak and Balaam
summary: Numbers places Balak and Balaam in Moab while Israel is camped on the plains east of Jericho.

name: Moses views the land from Nebo
summary: Deuteronomy ends with Moses viewing the land from Nebo/Pisgah and dying in Moab. The Nebo ridge is geographically clear; the exact summit and burial place are not.

name: Crossing the Jordan
summary: Joshua describes Israel crossing the Jordan opposite Jericho. The river corridor is mapped; an exact crossing point is not.

name: Fall of Jericho
summary: Joshua 6 narrates the fall of Jericho. Tell es-Sultan is securely Jericho, but correlation of its destruction history with the narrative is disputed.

name: Ai campaign
summary: Joshua 7–8 narrates defeat and later victory at Ai. The leading identification with et-Tell creates well-known chronological problems because the site was not a major occupied city in the conventional Late Bronze setting.

name: Gibeonite treaty and southern battle
summary: Joshua 9–10 links the treaty with Gibeon to a southern coalition and the battle associated with the Valley of Aijalon. Gibeon itself is securely located; reconstructed campaign lines are schematic.

name: Northern coalition and Hazor
summary: Joshua 11 makes Hazor the head of a northern coalition and says the city was burned. Tel Hazor is securely identified, but which archaeological destruction horizon, if any, corresponds to the narrative is debated.

name: Covenant ceremonies at Shechem
summary: Joshua 8 and 24 place covenantal ceremonies in the Shechem/Ebal/Gerizim setting. The mountains and ancient Shechem are geographically identifiable.

name: Assembly at Shiloh
summary: Joshua 18 places the tent of meeting and land-allotment assembly at Shiloh. Khirbet Seilun is securely ancient Shiloh; the sanctuary’s exact physical form is not identified.

name: Deborah, Barak, and Sisera
summary: Judges 4–5 locates the conflict across Kedesh, Mount Tabor, the Kishon, and the Jezreel/Esdraelon system. Exact troop movements remain reconstructive.

name: Gideon and Midian
summary: Judges 6–8 centers Gideon’s campaign in the Jezreel Valley and at the Spring of Harod before pursuit east of the Jordan. Several later route points are uncertain.

name: Jephthah and Ammon
summary: Judges 10–12 places Jephthah in Gilead and narrates conflict with Ammon. The broad Transjordan setting is clear; Mizpah and the campaign route are not securely mapped.

name: Samson on the Philistine frontier
summary: Judges 13–16 unfolds across Zorah, Timnah, the Sorek Valley, Ashkelon, and Gaza. Several smaller sites such as Lehi remain unknown.

name: Leviticus framed at Sinai
summary: Leviticus presents major priestly and covenant legislation as given to Moses at or in relation to Sinai. Because the mountain is unlocated, the atlas treats this as a textual setting rather than a mapped archaeological event site.

name: Othniel and the early Judges cycle
summary: Judges 3 presents Othniel as the first judge. His earlier capture of Debir is geographically relevant, but Debir itself remains disputed.

name: Ehud and Eglon of Moab
summary: Judges 3 situates Moabite domination around the City of Palms/Jericho and describes Ehud rallying Israel in the Ephraimite hill country. Exact palace and route locations are not recoverable.

name: Abimelech at Shechem and Thebez
summary: Judges 9 centers Abimelech’s rule and violence on Shechem, Mount Gerizim, and later Thebez. Shechem and Gerizim are secure geography; Thebez is mapped only as a candidate near Tubas.

name: Danite migration from the Shephelah to Laish
summary: Judges 18 narrates scouts and a migrating Danite group moving from the Zorah–Eshtaol district north to Laish, which is renamed Dan. Tel Dan is a secure geographic anchor; the exact route is reconstructed.

name: Gibeah outrage and Benjaminite civil war
summary: Judges 19–21 moves from Bethlehem to Gibeah and then to assemblies and battles involving Mizpah, Bethel, Gibeah, Jabesh-gilead, and Shiloh. Several site identifications vary in confidence.

name: Ruth and Naomi travel from Moab to Bethlehem
summary: Ruth 1 frames the story as a migration from Moab back to Bethlehem. The exact road is not described.

name: Samuel’s early life at Shiloh
summary: The Samuel narrative opens around the Shiloh sanctuary under Eli.

name: Ark captured in the Aphek–Ebenezer battle
summary: Israel camps at Ebenezer, Philistines at Aphek, and the ark is captured.

name: Ark moves through Philistine cities and returns to Israel
summary: The ark narrative moves from Ashdod to Gath and Ekron, then to Beth-shemesh and Kiriath-jearim.

name: Saul is publicly chosen and confirmed as king
summary: Samuel’s narratives associate Saul’s emergence with Mizpah, Gibeah, and a later confirmation at Gilgal.

name: Saul relieves Jabesh-gilead
summary: Saul summons Israel and defeats the Ammonite threat against Jabesh-gilead.

name: Jonathan attacks the Philistine outpost at Michmash
summary: 1 Samuel 13–14 places Saul near Geba/Michmash and describes Jonathan crossing the steep pass to attack a Philistine outpost.

name: Samuel anoints David at Bethlehem
summary: The narrative shifts to Bethlehem, where Samuel anoints David among Jesse’s sons.

name: David and Goliath in the Elah Valley
summary: Philistine and Israelite forces face each other between Socoh and Azekah; David confronts Goliath in the valley.

name: David’s fugitive years
summary: David moves through Gath, Adullam, Keilah, Ziph, Maon, En-gedi, and other refuges while evading Saul.
scripture: 1 Samuel 21 1 Samuel 22 1 Samuel 23 1 Samuel 24 1 Samuel 25 1 Samuel 26

name: David receives Ziklag from Achish
summary: David lives under Philistine patronage and uses Ziklag as a base before Saul’s death.

name: Saul at Endor and the final battle on Gilboa
summary: Before the Philistine battle, Saul consults a medium at Endor; he and his sons die on Mount Gilboa, and their bodies are displayed at Beth-shean.

name: David becomes king at Hebron
summary: After Saul’s death, David moves to Hebron and reigns over Judah before gaining wider kingship.

name: Abner and Joab clash at Gibeon
summary: Forces aligned with Ish-bosheth and David meet at the pool of Gibeon during the civil conflict.

name: David captures Jerusalem / the stronghold of Zion
summary: David takes the Jebusite stronghold and makes Jerusalem his political center, naming the captured stronghold the City of David in the narrative.

name: David brings the ark toward Jerusalem
summary: The ark moves from Kiriath-jearim and is eventually installed in David’s city.

name: David confronts Philistine forces near Jerusalem
summary: Philistine forces spread through the Valley of Rephaim; David’s victories include the named but unlocated Baal-perazim.

name: Rabbah campaign and the Bathsheba narrative
summary: Joab campaigns against Rabbah while David remains in Jerusalem, forming the geographic frame of 2 Samuel 11–12.

name: Absalom’s revolt drives David from Jerusalem
summary: David crosses the Kidron, ascends the Mount of Olives, and ultimately reaches the Mahanaim area; the final battle is in the unlocated Forest of Ephraim.

name: David builds an altar at Araunah’s threshing floor
summary: After the census plague, David purchases the threshing floor and builds an altar; Chronicles later links this place to Solomon’s temple.

name: Solomon is anointed at Gihon
summary: Zadok and Nathan take Solomon to Gihon, where he is anointed during the succession crisis.

name: Solomon worships at Gibeon
summary: 1 Kings depicts Solomon sacrificing at the great high place at Gibeon before his dream.

name: Construction and dedication of the First Temple
summary: Kings and Chronicles describe Solomon’s temple construction and dedication in Jerusalem.
scripture: 1 Kings 5 1 Kings 6 1 Kings 7:13–51 1 Kings 8 2 Chronicles 2 2 Chronicles 3 2 Chronicles 5 2 Chronicles 7

name: Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer in the building program
summary: 1 Kings 9:15 names Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer in Solomon’s building levy. All three are major archaeological sites, but dating and royal attribution of particular monumental gates are debated.

name: Phoenician exchange with Tyre
summary: The Solomon narratives describe timber, craftsmen, and maritime cooperation with Hiram of Tyre.

name: The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon
summary: 1 Kings and Chronicles narrate a royal visit from Sheba to Jerusalem. Southern Arabia is the strongest broad cultural context, but no exact itinerary is recoverable.

name: The monarchy divides at Shechem
summary: Rehoboam’s assembly at Shechem ends with the northern tribes rejecting Davidic rule; Jeroboam becomes king over Israel while Judah remains under Rehoboam.
date: c. 930 BCE (conventional early divided-monarchy chronology)

name: Jeroboam’s Bethel and Dan sanctuaries
summary: Kings associates Jeroboam I with royal cult centers at Bethel and Dan. Both places are mappable; specific ritual installations require site-by-site archaeological interpretation.

name: Shoshenq I / biblical Shishak campaigns in the Levant
summary: Kings and Chronicles describe Shishak’s attack during Rehoboam’s reign; Shoshenq I’s Karnak relief independently attests an Egyptian Levantine campaign.
date: late 10th century BCE; commonly placed around 925 BCE

name: Omri founds Samaria
summary: Omri purchases the hill of Samaria and establishes a new northern capital.
date: early 9th century BCE

name: Battle of Qarqar
summary: Shalmaneser III’s Kurkh Monolith records a major coalition battle at Qarqar and names Ahab of Israel among the coalition. Kings does not narrate this battle.
date: 853 BCE

name: Mesha and Moab rebel against Israel
summary: 2 Kings 3 narrates a coalition campaign against Moab after Mesha rebels. The Mesha Stele independently presents Moabite liberation from Omride domination from a Moabite royal perspective.

name: Naboth’s vineyard at Jezreel
summary: 1 Kings 21 places Naboth’s vineyard beside Ahab’s Jezreel property and narrates its seizure through royal abuse.

name: Elijah, drought, Kerith, and Zarephath
summary: The Elijah cycle opens with drought, an unlocated brook east of the Jordan, and a stay in Phoenician Zarephath.

name: Elijah’s confrontation on Mount Carmel
summary: 1 Kings 18 places the contest involving Elijah and prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, followed by rain and movement toward Jezreel.

name: Elijah flees toward Horeb
summary: After the Carmel narrative, Elijah travels via Beersheba into the wilderness and reaches Horeb, “the mountain of God.”

name: Elijah’s departure and Elisha’s succession
summary: 2 Kings 2 moves through Bethel, Jericho, and the Jordan in the transition from Elijah to Elisha.

name: Naaman washes in the Jordan
summary: 2 Kings 5 places the Aramean commander Naaman in an Israel-Aram diplomatic/prophetic narrative culminating in washing in the Jordan.

name: Jehu’s coup reaches Jezreel and Samaria
summary: Jehu is anointed amid the Ramoth-gilead war and rapidly seizes the northern throne, killing Joram and Jezebel at Jezreel before consolidating power in Samaria.
date: mid-9th century BCE; Jehu’s accession conventionally c. 841 BCE

name: Assyrian monument depicts tribute from Jehu
summary: Shalmaneser III’s Black Obelisk includes a tribute scene captioned with Jehu under the Assyrian dynastic label of Omri.
date: c. 841 BCE tribute episode

name: Hazael pressures Israel and Judah
summary: Kings portrays Hazael of Damascus taking territory from Israel and later capturing Gath and threatening Jerusalem.

name: Athaliah’s rule and Joash’s accession
summary: The Jerusalem court narrative moves through Athaliah’s seizure of power, Joash’s preservation, and his later public enthronement at the temple.

name: Amos confronts the priest of Bethel
summary: Amos 7 places a confrontation between Amos and Amaziah at Bethel, linking a Judean prophet with a northern royal sanctuary.
date: mid-8th century BCE prophetic setting

name: Hosea addresses the Northern Kingdom before its fall
summary: Hosea’s oracles repeatedly invoke Ephraim, Israel, Samaria, and Bethel/Beth-aven in the decades of political instability before Assyrian conquest.

name: Jonah narrative: Joppa, the sea, and Nineveh
summary: The book of Jonah contrasts an attempted voyage from Joppa toward disputed Tarshish with a divine commission to Nineveh.

name: Syro-Ephraimite crisis
summary: Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel pressure Judah; Ahaz appeals to Tiglath-pileser III, while Isaiah 7 frames the crisis in Jerusalem.

name: Tiglath-pileser III annexes northern territories
summary: Assyrian expansion under Tiglath-pileser III captures Damascus and parts of northern Israel; Kings records deportations from Galilee and Transjordan.
date: 734–732 BCE western campaigns

name: Siege and fall of Samaria
summary: Kings attributes the siege’s beginning to Shalmaneser V and reports Samaria’s capture after three years; Sargon II later claims the conquest and deportation in his own inscriptions.
date: siege/fall around 724–722 BCE; Sargon’s claims continue after accession

name: Assyrian deportations from the Northern Kingdom
summary: Kings names Halah, the Habor/Khabur region of Gozan, and cities of the Medes as deportation destinations after Samaria’s fall.
date: late 8th century BCE

name: Hezekiah’s reform program
summary: Kings and Chronicles associate Hezekiah with centralizing/reforming worship in Judah and removing cultic objects and high places.

name: Jerusalem waterworks and the Siloam Tunnel
summary: Biblical texts credit Hezekiah with major waterworks; the Siloam Tunnel and its inscription provide a dramatic archaeological context for Iron Age Jerusalem engineering.
date: late 8th century BCE context

name: Sennacherib captures Lachish
summary: In 701 BCE the Assyrian army captures Lachish. Archaeology, Assyrian reliefs, inscriptions, and biblical references converge unusually strongly on this event.
date: 701 BCE

name: Sennacherib’s 701 BCE pressure on Jerusalem
summary: Biblical narratives describe Assyrian demands and Jerusalem’s deliverance. Sennacherib’s annals report devastating Judah and confining Hezekiah in Jerusalem while claiming tribute, but do not claim the city’s capture.
date: 701 BCE

name: Micah’s Shephelah and Jerusalem horizon
summary: Micah 1 names a chain of towns in Judah’s Shephelah and addresses both Samaria and Jerusalem in the shadow of imperial crisis.

name: Manasseh of Judah in the Assyrian imperial world
summary: Manasseh’s long reign belongs to a Judah deeply embedded in Neo-Assyrian power; Assyrian royal lists independently name him as king of Judah.
date: Seventh century BCE; regnal reconstructions vary because co-regency models differ

name: Amon’s short reign and assassination
summary: Kings and Chronicles describe a brief reign of Amon between Manasseh and Josiah.
date: c. 642–640 BCE (conventional chronology)

name: Zephaniah’s horizon: Judah, the coast, Transjordan, Cush, and Nineveh
summary: Zephaniah’s oracles create a late seventh-century geographic horizon stretching from Jerusalem across neighboring peoples to Assyria.
date: Josiah’s reign, late seventh century BCE

name: Nineveh falls to the Babylonian-Median coalition
summary: Nineveh, core capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, is captured and devastated in 612 BCE.
date: 612 BCE

name: Nahum’s oracle concerning Nineveh
summary: Nahum announces judgment on Nineveh and compares it with Thebes/No-Amon, which Assyria had conquered earlier.
date: Late seventh century BCE context; exact composition date debated

name: Habakkuk and the rise of the Chaldeans
summary: Habakkuk 1 invokes the Chaldeans/Babylonians as a terrifying military force in a prophetic dialogue about violence and justice.
date: Late seventh to early sixth century BCE is commonly proposed

name: Lamentations remembers Jerusalem’s catastrophe
summary: Lamentations poetically mourns a destroyed, depopulated Jerusalem and the collapse of Zion/temple life.
date: Exilic context after the 587/586 BCE destruction

name: Obadiah’s oracle against Edom
summary: Obadiah condemns Edom for violence and opportunism connected with Jerusalem’s disaster and invokes Mount Esau/Teman geography.
date: Date disputed; often placed in exilic or early post-exilic context

name: Malachi’s temple-and-priesthood setting in Persian Yehud
summary: Malachi addresses a functioning temple cult, priesthood, offerings, and a “governor,” fitting the Persian-period Yehud world after temple restoration.
date: Persian period, after a functioning Second Temple; exact date debated

name: Josiah dies in the Megiddo campaign context
summary: Kings and Chronicles place Josiah’s death in connection with Pharaoh Necho II at Megiddo as Egypt moves north toward the Euphrates corridor.
date: 609 BCE (conventional historical chronology)

name: Battle of Carchemish and Babylonian ascendance
summary: Babylonian forces under Nebuchadnezzar defeat Egypt’s army at Carchemish, reshaping control of Syria-Palestine.
date: 605 BCE

name: Jeremiah’s scroll read and burned
summary: Jeremiah 36 depicts Baruch reading a prophetic scroll that King Jehoiakim cuts and burns, after which it is rewritten.
date: During Jehoiakim’s reign; Jeremiah 36 specifies the fourth/fifth-year sequence

name: Nebuchadnezzar captures Jerusalem and deports Jehoiachin
summary: Jerusalem is taken, Jehoiachin is deported, and Zedekiah is installed. Babylonian chronicle evidence independently anchors the capture in 597 BCE.
date: 597 BCE

name: Jehoiachin appears in Babylonian ration tablets
summary: Administrative tablets from Babylonia name Yaukin, king of Judah, and members of his household, independently attesting the exiled royal family.
date: Sixth century BCE, during Nebuchadnezzar II’s reign

name: Lachish letters in Judah’s final crisis
summary: Hebrew ostraca from Lachish illuminate military communication and anxiety near the end of the kingdom.
date: Early sixth century BCE, near Judah’s final Babylonian crisis

name: Jerusalem and the First Temple are destroyed
summary: After Zedekiah’s rebellion, Babylonian forces breach Jerusalem, burn the temple/palace/major buildings, dismantle defenses, and deport more inhabitants.
date: 587/586 BCE (chronological convention varies)

name: Zedekiah flees, is captured near Jericho, and taken to Riblah
summary: Kings and Jeremiah describe Zedekiah escaping Jerusalem toward the Arabah, being captured in the plains of Jericho, and brought to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah.
date: During Jerusalem’s final fall, 587/586 BCE

name: Gedaliah governs from Mizpah
summary: After Jerusalem’s destruction, Babylon appoints Gedaliah over the population remaining in Judah; the biblical narrative locates his administration at Mizpah.
date: Immediately after Jerusalem’s destruction

name: Gedaliah is assassinated at Mizpah
summary: Ishmael son of Nethaniah kills Gedaliah, precipitating further instability and the movement of survivors toward Egypt.
date: Shortly after 587/586 BCE

name: Judean survivors go to Egypt
summary: After Gedaliah’s assassination, Johanan and the group with Jeremiah travel into Egypt, reaching Tahpanhes according to Jeremiah.
date: Early Babylonian period after Jerusalem’s fall

name: Ezekiel receives his opening vision by the Kebar
summary: Ezekiel dates his prophetic call among the exiles by the Kebar in the fifth year of Jehoiachin’s exile.
date: c. 593/592 BCE (fifth year of Jehoiachin’s exile)

name: Ezekiel’s vision of Jerusalem and the temple
summary: Ezekiel 8–11 presents a visionary transport from Babylonia to Jerusalem, culminating in departure of divine glory.
date: Sixth year of Jehoiachin’s exile in Ezekiel’s chronology

name: Judean communities documented in Babylonian tablets
summary: Cuneiform archives such as Al-Yahudu document Judeans living, farming, contracting, and serving obligations in Babylonia across generations.
date: Documents span the sixth–fifth centuries BCE

name: Daniel’s Babylonian court setting
summary: Daniel 1 places Daniel and his companions in a Babylonian royal educational/court setting under Nebuchadnezzar.
date: Daniel 1’s Babylonian court setting

name: Belshazzar’s banquet and the fall-of-Babylon literary setting
summary: Daniel 5 sets its banquet on the night Babylon changes hands and names Belshazzar, a historically attested royal son/co-regent figure.
date: Literary setting aligned with Babylon’s fall in 539 BCE

name: Babylon falls to Cyrus’s forces
summary: The Achaemenid conquest of Babylon ends Neo-Babylonian rule and establishes Persian control of Mesopotamia.
date: 539 BCE

name: Cyrus’s Babylonian restoration program
summary: The Cyrus Cylinder presents Cyrus as restoring cults and returning divine images/communities within Mesopotamian royal ideology after 539 BCE.
date: After the conquest of Babylon, 539 BCE

name: Ezra credits Cyrus with authorizing temple restoration
summary: Ezra 1 presents Cyrus issuing an authorization for rebuilding the house of YHWH in Jerusalem and returning temple vessels.
date: c. 538/537 BCE in conventional reconstruction

name: Return community and altar/temple foundation traditions
summary: Ezra describes returnees from Babylonian exile, restoration of the altar, and temple rebuilding associated with Zerubbabel and Jeshua.
date: Early Persian period, late sixth century BCE

name: Haggai and Zechariah urge temple rebuilding
summary: Dated prophetic activity under Darius I centers on Jerusalem’s temple restoration and the leadership of Zerubbabel and Joshua/Jeshua.
date: 520–518 BCE for the principal dated Haggai/early Zechariah material

name: Second Temple completed in Darius I’s reign
summary: Ezra dates completion of the rebuilt Jerusalem temple to the sixth year of Darius I.
date: 515 BCE (conventional conversion of Darius I year 6)

name: Esther’s Susa court narrative
summary: Esther’s story unfolds at the Persian royal center of Susa and across the empire under Ahasuerus, commonly identified with Xerxes I.
date: If Ahasuerus is Xerxes I: reign 486–465 BCE

name: Ezra leads a group from Babylonia to Jerusalem
summary: Ezra 7–8 describes departure from Babylonia, assembly at the unlocated Ahava, and arrival at Jerusalem with royal authorization and temple gifts.
date: Traditionally 458 BCE; alternate chronologies place Ezra later

name: Nehemiah travels from Susa to Jerusalem
summary: Nehemiah receives news at Susa, obtains royal permission from Artaxerxes, and travels to Jerusalem as governor.
date: 445/444 BCE (Artaxerxes I year 20, conventional chronology)

name: Jerusalem’s walls rebuilt in Nehemiah
summary: Nehemiah 2–6 narrates survey, organized rebuilding, opposition, and completion of Jerusalem’s wall in fifty-two days.
date: Mid-fifth century BCE in conventional Nehemiah chronology

name: Ezra reads the Torah in Jerusalem
summary: Nehemiah 8 depicts Ezra reading and interpreting the Torah before an assembly in Jerusalem.
date: Persian period; relative sequence within Ezra–Nehemiah is debated

name: Elephantine community petitions about its YHW temple
summary: Aramaic correspondence from Elephantine describes the local YHW temple and petitions authorities for permission to rebuild it after destruction.
date: 407 BCE temple petition

name: Ramat Rahel continues as an administrative center
summary: Archaeology indicates continued administrative importance at Ramat Rahel across Babylonian and Persian rule.
date: Babylonian through Persian-period phases

name: Jehoiachin released from prison in Babylon
summary: The closing scene of 2 Kings says Evil-merodach/Amel-Marduk elevates Jehoiachin in Babylon in the thirty-seventh year of his exile.
date: c. 561 BCE (conventional conversion of Jehoiachin’s 37th exile year)

name: Alexander conquers the Levantine coast
summary: Alexander’s campaign moved through the eastern Mediterranean coast in 332 BCE, including the sieges of Tyre and Gaza before Egypt.
date: 332 BCE

name: Alexander founds Alexandria
summary: Alexander entered Egypt in 332 BCE and founded Alexandria in 331 BCE in conventional chronology.
date: 331 BCE (conventional foundation date)

name: Judea in the Ptolemaic sphere
summary: After the Successor struggles, Judea formed part of the Ptolemaic-controlled southern Levant for much of the third century BCE.
date: Third century BCE; broadly 301–200 BCE for sustained Ptolemaic control

name: Greek Torah / Septuagint translation context
summary: The Greek translation of the Torah emerged in Hellenistic Egypt, conventionally associated with Alexandria in the third century BCE.
date: Third century BCE; exact stages debated

name: Battle of Panium and Seleucid takeover
summary: Antiochus III defeated Ptolemaic forces near Panium around 200 BCE, shifting Coele-Syria and Judea into the Seleucid sphere.
date: 200 BCE (commonly dated)

name: Seleucid temple-administration context under Seleucus IV
summary: Inscriptional evidence from the reign of Seleucus IV illuminates royal administrative involvement in temple finances across Coele-Syria/Phoenicia.
date: c. 178 BCE administrative context

name: Antiochus IV and the Jerusalem crisis
summary: Ancient Jewish sources describe severe intervention in Jerusalem, plundering, cultic disruption and decrees restricting traditional practices under Antiochus IV.
date: 169–167 BCE crisis sequence

name: Maccabean revolt begins at Modein
summary: 1 Maccabees locates the outbreak of armed resistance at Modein under Mattathias, conventionally around 167 BCE.
date: 167 BCE (conventional chronology)

name: Battle of Emmaus
summary: Judas Maccabeus defeated a Seleucid force in the Emmaus region, conventionally dated to 165 BCE.
date: 165 BCE (conventional chronology)

name: Rededication of the Jerusalem temple
summary: Judas and his supporters rededicated the temple after recapturing Jerusalem, remembered in the festival of Hanukkah.
date: 164 BCE

name: Battle of Beth-zechariah
summary: A Seleucid army under Antiochus V’s government defeated Judas’s forces near Beth-zechariah; 1 Maccabees famously associates the battle with war elephants.
date: 162 BCE (conventional chronology)

name: Defeat of Nicanor near Adasa
summary: Judas Maccabeus defeated Nicanor in a battle near Adasa, conventionally dated to 161 BCE.
date: 161 BCE

name: Death of Judas at Elasa
summary: Judas Maccabeus was killed fighting Bacchides at Elasa.
date: 160 BCE

name: Jonathan becomes high priest
summary: Jonathan Apphus received the high priesthood amid Seleucid dynastic competition.
date: 152 BCE

name: Simon and effective Judean independence
summary: Under Simon, tribute obligations were remitted and Judean rule became effectively independent from Seleucid control; the Acra garrison was removed shortly afterward.
date: 142–141 BCE transition

name: Hasmonean incorporation of Idumea
summary: Josephus associates John Hyrcanus with the conquest/incorporation of Idumean centers including Adora and Marisa and with compulsory adoption of Judean customs.
date: c. 125 BCE, approximate

name: Destruction of the Mount Gerizim sanctuary under John Hyrcanus
summary: Josephus credits John Hyrcanus with destroying the Samaritan sanctuary on Mount Gerizim; archaeology documents a major Hellenistic sanctuary and destruction/transition.
date: c. 111/110 BCE, conventional reconstruction

name: Hasmonean kingship under Aristobulus I

name: Alexander Jannaeus expands the Hasmonean kingdom

name: Reign of Salome Alexandra

date: 76–67 BCE (conventional chronology)

name: Hasmonean civil war
summary: Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II contested the throne, drawing in Nabataean and then Roman power.

name: Pompey captures Jerusalem
summary: Pompey intervened in the Hasmonean conflict and captured Jerusalem after a siege in 63 BCE, ending independent Hasmonean kingship.
date: 63 BCE

name: Roman provincial reorganization in Syria
summary: Pompey reorganized former Seleucid territories into Roman Syria, fundamentally changing the political environment around Judea.
date: 64/63 BCE transition

name: Caesar, Hyrcanus II, and Antipater

date: 47 BCE context

name: Parthian intervention and Antigonus II

date: 40 BCE

name: Rome appoints Herod king
summary: The Roman Senate recognized Herod as king in 40 BCE, although he still had to conquer the kingdom militarily.
date: 40 BCE

name: Herod captures Jerusalem
summary: With Roman support, Herod captured Jerusalem in 37 BCE and Antigonus II was removed, beginning effective Herodian rule.
date: 37 BCE

name: Battle of Actium
summary: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, transforming the eastern Mediterranean patronage system on which Herod had depended.
date: 31 BCE

name: Herod meets Octavian after Actium
summary: Josephus describes Herod meeting Octavian on Rhodes and successfully retaining his kingship after Antony’s defeat.
date: 30 BCE, conventional chronology

name: Herod begins major Temple Mount expansion
summary: Herod launched a major rebuilding and enlargement of the Jerusalem temple complex, conventionally dated to 20/19 BCE.
date: 20/19 BCE commencement, conventional chronology

name: Herod’s Caesarea and harbor mature

date: c. 10–9 BCE dedication/completion phase

name: Qumran settlement and manuscript-cave context
summary: Khirbet Qumran flourished in the late Second Temple period near caves containing a diverse manuscript corpus now known as the Dead Sea Scrolls.
date: Late second/first centuries BCE into the first century CE; phases debated

name: Jewish temple at Leontopolis in Egypt
summary: Josephus describes a Jewish temple in Egypt associated with Onias, providing an important example of Second Temple-period Jewish diversity outside Jerusalem.
date: Second century BCE; foundation chronology debated

name: Birth of Jesus in Bethlehem

date: commonly placed c. 6–4 BCE; exact year disputed

name: Magi and Herod in Matthew

date: within Matthew’s Herod the Great setting, before 4 BCE

name: Flight into Egypt
summary: Matthew narrates Joseph taking Mary and Jesus from Bethlehem into Egypt and later returning. No Egyptian town or exact route is named.
date: Matthew infancy narrative; before death of Herod the Great

name: Jesus’ family at Nazareth
summary: Matthew and Luke both associate Jesus’ upbringing with Nazareth, though their infancy narrative sequences differ.

name: John the Baptist in the wilderness and Jordan
summary: The Synoptics place John in the Judean wilderness/Jordan region calling for repentance and baptizing; John’s Gospel also names Bethany beyond the Jordan and Aenon near Salim.
date: early first century CE; precise start year debated

name: Baptism of Jesus
summary: The Gospel traditions place Jesus’ baptism by John in the Jordan. The exact place on the river is not identified in the canonical texts.
date: early ministry; exact year uncertain

name: Temptation in the wilderness
summary: The Synoptics place Jesus in the wilderness after the baptism but do not name a specific mountain, cave, or modern site.

name: John the Baptist imprisoned and executed

name: Wedding at Cana

name: Capernaum as a Galilean ministry center

name: Sermon on the Mount — unnamed mountain

name: Crossing and storm on the Sea of Galilee

name: Jesus in Samaria at Sychar

name: Widow’s son at Nain
summary: Luke locates a raising narrative at Nain in Galilee.

name: Transfiguration on an unnamed high mountain

name: Lazarus of Bethany narrative

name: Jesus and Zacchaeus at Jericho
summary: Luke places the encounter with Zacchaeus during Jesus’ passage through Jericho.

name: Anointing at Bethany
summary: Mark, Matthew, and John place an anointing tradition at Bethany, with narrative details differing among the accounts.

name: Last Supper in an upper room
summary: The Synoptic Passion narratives place the meal in a prepared upper room within Jerusalem; the exact building is not identified.

name: Prayer and arrest at Gethsemane
summary: The Synoptics place Jesus’ prayer and arrest at Gethsemane; John describes a garden across the Kidron.

name: Hearings before Annas / Caiaphas
summary: The Gospel Passion traditions place Jesus before high-priestly authorities in Jerusalem, but the precise houses and sequence vary among accounts.

summary: Luke alone narrates Pilate sending Jesus to Herod Antipas, who was in Jerusalem at the time.

name: Road to Emmaus
summary: Luke narrates two disciples traveling from Jerusalem to Emmaus and returning. The village’s location is disputed.

name: Galilee resurrection appearance traditions

name: Caiaphas as high priest
summary: Joseph Caiaphas held the high priesthood during much of Pilate’s prefecture and appears prominently in the Passion narratives.

name: Herod Antipas rules Galilee and Perea
summary: After Herod the Great’s death, Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch and developed Tiberias as a capital.
date: 4 BCE–39 CE

name: Archelaus rules Judea, Samaria, and Idumea
summary: Archelaus inherited a large portion of Herod’s kingdom before Rome deposed him and converted his territory to direct provincial administration.

name: Ascension narrative from the Mount of Olives

name: Matthias chosen among the Twelve
summary: Acts places the selection of Matthias within the Jerusalem community before Pentecost.

name: Pentecost in Jerusalem
summary: Acts 2 narrates the Spirit coming upon the gathered disciples during Pentecost and a multilingual crowd in Jerusalem.

name: Healing at the Beautiful Gate
summary: Acts 3 places Peter and John at a gate called Beautiful and then Solomon’s Portico.

name: Stephen’s speech and stoning

name: Philip in Samaria
summary: Acts 8 narrates Philip preaching in a city of Samaria before later travel south.

name: Philip and the Ethiopian official on the Gaza road
summary: Acts places the encounter on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza, described as desert/deserted. The exact road segment is unknown.

name: Saul’s Damascus-road encounter and entry into Damascus

date: commonly placed c. 33–36 CE

name: Paul’s visit to “Arabia” in Galatians

name: Paul’s escape from Damascus

name: Peter and Cornelius at Caesarea
summary: Acts 10–11 links Peter at Joppa with Cornelius at Caesarea in a pivotal Gentile-inclusion narrative.

name: Agrippa I persecutes Jerusalem leaders
summary: Acts 12 says Agrippa I executes James son of Zebedee and imprisons Peter.

name: Paul stoned at Lystra

name: Jerusalem Council / apostolic meeting
summary: Acts 15 narrates a Jerusalem meeting over Gentile inclusion and Torah obligations.

name: Thessalonica and Berea
